title: As schedule gets more difficult, sustained momentum key for Raiders
summary: Klint Kubiak and his desert marauders passed the first test of the 2026 campaign by drubbing the visiting Miami Dolphins this past Sunday. Widely considered a “gimmie” game due to the Dolphins being in the midst of a tear down and rebuild with a new general manager and head coach, the 27-13 victory was in-line […]
full_text: (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Klint Kubiak and his desert marauders passed the first test of the 2026 campaign by drubbing the visiting Miami Dolphins this past Sunday. Widely considered a “gimmie” game due to the Dolphins being in the midst of a tear down and rebuild with a new general manager and head coach, the 27-13 victory was in-line with many expectations. In Week 2 and beyond, however, Kubiak’s Las Vegas Raiders embark on a five-game slate that features superior competition than what Miami offered within the confines of Allegiant Stadium. Over the next five games, the Silver & Black lock horns with the Los Angeles Chargers, New Orleans Saints, Kansas City Chiefs, New England Patriots, Buffalo Bills, before bookending with the Los Angeles Rams on October 25. While some may be quick to dismiss the season-opening matchup against a downtrodden Miami squad, that upcoming slate for Las Vegas isn’t easily as banished. But it was only natural for Kubiak to field a question earlier this week on playing top-level competition as the Raiders enter what’s considered a tough stretch of their 2026 schedule. “Yes. I mean, you learn something new every day in practice. You learn something new during the games. It’s a lot more stress going on. You learn a lot about your coaches too. You learn about your training staff, your strength staff. You learn about everybody in this pressure cooker that we work in, and that’s what makes the NFL so fun,” Kubiak responded during his media session this past Monday. “So yes, there’s a tough stretch coming up because that’s what the NFL is, but we just try to look one game at a time.” That singular game focus per week is apt for a rookie head coach and his rebuilding football team. But being dismissive of the Raiders’ victory just because they played the rebuilding Dolphins has its pitfalls. Especially considering the Silver & Black surmounted instances where previous variants of the Raiders would’ve folded. "We're building a new culture and that's a culture that's going to win football games." – Ashton Jeanty "Klint (Kubiak) has talked about it, this stadium we have to make it ours and it starts with winning." – Maxx Crosby #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/DzI4xkYvT9 — Vince Sapienza (@VinceSapienza) September 14, 2026 Whether you want to label it quicksand or an avalanche, when things have gone awry, Las Vegas habitually wilted against the mounting pressure instead of rising to the occasion. The jury is most definitely still out on this for Kubiak’s and general manager John Spytek’s rendition of the Raiders, however, against Miami, positive signs of potential change were present. From an outstanding pure hustle play by practice squad call-up Cody White that kept a long 79-yard kickoff return from becoming a touchdown that inspired the defense to rise up and force a field goal — which was missed by the Dolphins, by the way. But responding to the Dolphins’ interception and ensuing touchdown on the next drive after the lead was slashed to 17-13 in the third quarter, too. In the past, that was a pivotal turning point where the Raiders couldn’t dig themselves out of. But Kubiak and Co. showed resilience and resolve to respond with a touchdown of their own. And that’s what this variant of the Silver & Black must make a habit of if it wants to succeed with a winning culture change. “Yeah, that’s the expectation. When things don’t go your way, then you have the ability to change it, instead of sitting there and feeling sorry for yourselves, and you’ve got to change your own fortunes, and that’s what we expect from our guys,” Kubiak said when asked how much he appreciated the way the team responded after the Dolphins’ takeaway and touchdown. “Yeah, you’re right. They come fast. We got to build on what we did well this last week, knowing that we have an extremely good opponent coming,” Kubiak added during his media availability this past Wednesday, reminding folk of the one-game-at-a-time approach. “We’re going there. Every week in the NFL is a completely new season. It’s 17 one-game seasons.” The best play call of Week 1 belongs to Klint Kubiak! @Filmwatchers1 breaks down how Ashton Jeanty scored a wide open touchdown ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/EAMK9g5mem — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) September 15, 2026 Keep Doing This Kubiak’s affinity for the fullback position was something that stood out to me long before the Raiders hired him as the new head coach earlier this offseason. It’s a position that’s seen less and less in the modern NFL but was a traditional spot on the Raiders roster up until the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Kubiak was quick to sync with Spytek to get a “true” fullback on the roster and in free agency, the team pried away Connor Heyward from the Pittsburgh Steelers. And in the Week 1 win, we got an excellent example of the value the fullback brings to Kubiak’s offense — specifically — Kirk Cousins’ 13-yard touchdown pass to a wide open Ashton Jeanty in the third quarter. Play action was dialed up and in the video above, you can see Heyward charging towards the gap and Dolphins linebackers react. But Heyward submarines one defender with a cut block and the aftermath prevented the other linebacker to chase and cover Jeanty — wide open, six points. “Yeah, I think Connor had a really solid showing,” said Kubiak of his fullback. “That’s what we have come to expect from him. I think when he came into the game, the thing about a fullback is that the picture always changes post-snap. You are the cleanup guy; someone misses a block, you’ve got to be Johnny on the Spot. We mis-target something, you’ve got to make the offensive line right. But him using his brain and then him getting guys on the ground stood out.” Heyward played 32 snaps on offense, which is 47 percent of the team’s total of 68 against Miami. He also notched eight snaps on special teams. And it’ll be interesting to see how the 27-year-old’s snap counts fluctuate or remain stable as the season progresses. Quote of Note “I think it’s just staying true to who we are, playing our style, playing with a shocking operation, everything that we talk about, and just staying true to our fundamentals. Whether it’s snap one, snap 50, snap however many it takes in that game, but just staying true to our fundamentals and executing what’s called.” —Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on what the Raiders are working on this week regarding finishing games better

title: What happened in Los Angeles Chargers’ upset loss ahead of matchup with Las Vegas Raiders?
summary: While they count the same in each team’s overall record, divisional games always have more on the line in the NFL. That’s especially true in the Week 2 AFC West matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers, with the Chargers falling to the Arizona Cardinals during the season opener. To preview the […]
full_text: (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images While they count the same in each team’s overall record, divisional games always have more on the line in the NFL. That’s especially true in the Week 2 AFC West matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and Los Angeles Chargers , with the Chargers falling to the Arizona Cardinals during the season opener. To preview the game, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our frenemies, Bolts from the Blue , and Michael Peterson was kind enough to answer a few questions about Los Angeles for Raider Nation. Q: The Chargers were widely considered contenders heading into the season but were on the wrong side of the biggest Week 1 upset. To put it simply: What happened? Has that changed expectations and/or the optimism surrounding the team? A: Well, to put it bluntly, everything went wrong in all three phases of the game as the Chargers looked incredibly sloppy and seemingly had no answers for what was supposed to be one of the worst teams in the NFL this season. New defensive coordinator Chris O’Leary looked out of his depth calling the defense, and that’s wild to think after they were a top-five unit under Jesse Minter from 2024-2025. The Cardinals stressed their zone defense with quick, efficient passes, and Brissett looked incredibly comfortable making the right pass over and over again. He had the answers to the test, seemingly, and the Chargers couldn’t do anything to pressure him quickly enough before the ball was out to Trey McBride or Kendrick Bourne, both of whom could not be stopped. Offensively, the first drive looked exactly like we expected under Mike McDaniel. Justin Herbert was crisp in finding Ladd McConkey three times before Omarion Hampton broke multiple tackles en route to the end zone to cap it all off. THAT was what everyone was waiting for. But…then it all fell apart. After the Cards missed a field goal, the Bolts had all the momentum in the world until Hampton ran into the back of wideout Tre’ Harris and the ball popped loose for an Arizona recovery. From there, the entire group looked disjointed, and the interior of the offensive line was once again the prime suspect in killing drive after drive. No run game was had. Herbert and his receivers were never on the same page again, and it looked even worse after McConkey left with an injury. My expectations have changed, and I believe rightfully so. It’s important not to overreact after just one game, but I’m taking into account just how bad that one game was. If it was that bad against a team like that, then what is the whole operation going to look like when they start facing other AFC powers? How can I be confident that this team will go back to “contender” after that mess on Sunday? Right now, I’m in “prove it” mode going forward. If the Chargers are a contender, then they’ll play like one and start winning games. If not, then they deserve all the negative coverage that will follow from not living up to the self-imposed expectations. Q: Building on the question above, Los Angeles seemingly upgraded its offensive coordinator in the offseason, going from Greg Roman to Mike McDaniel. However, the results aren’t there yet, with a 14-point performance in the season opener. What needs to change for McDaniel’s offense to function properly moving forward? A: Herbert and his receivers need to be on the same page. Plain and simple. Quentin Johnston showed little effort when targeted and was disconnected from Herbert most of the day. The interior offensive line also needs to improve tremendously, and that also includes NOT platooning the left guard spot when Kayode Awosika was light-years better than Trey Pipkins. There HAS to be some semblance of a run game, and if you can’t perform better than last year’s group that was held together by bubble gum and sticks, then the system needs to be thrown away and rebooted. Q: From an outsider’s perspective, it kind of feels like this is a “now or never” type of season for Justin Herbert. He’s plenty talented, but there aren’t a lot of quarterbacks who start for one team for as long as he has without any postseason success. Derek Carr is one exception to that, but even Carr was a polarizing player within Raider Nation toward the end of his tenure. So, I’m curious about the perception of Herbert heading into this season? A: You’re absolutely correct that this does feel like a “now or never” season with Herbert. At this rate, he’s had as many super productive seasons passing the ball as he has had fairly average seasons, and this year with McDaniel was supposed to get him back to chucking the ball around the yard and putting up video game numbers like he did in 2020, 2021, and 2022. With the way this past Sunday looked, I don’t know if that’s on the table anymore. The problem is, there are so many quarterbacks starting in the league that are worse than Herbert, and even Herbert’s bad games are better than most above-average performances. I don’t think Herbert’s job is in jeopardy, even if they don’t make the playoffs. He normally takes care of what he can control, and that’s why there is such a force supporting him despite the lack of postseason success. Overall, I thought he did everything he could against the Cardinals until he threw that interception. It made no sense. It was so bad that I don’t think anyone can get behind the decision. It was a small receiver being double-covered, and Herbert did not have to force the throw at all. There was plenty of time, and it wasn’t third or fourth down. It seriously looked like another quarterback was on the field in that moment because it was so uncharacteristic of him. Right now, Herbert has the majority of the fan base behind him. If more games like Sunday continue to stack up, then I have to acknowledge that support may fade faster than expected. Q: New defensive coordinator Chris O’Leary has taken over for Jesse Minter in Los Angeles, but O’Leary had a rough debut last week against the Cardinals. The Chargers gave up 393 yards, which would have been the second-most they surrendered last season. Do you think that was more of a scheme or personnel issue, or some combination of the two? Who needs to step up moving forward? A: It truly looked like O’Leary was not prepared for the task. Brissett looked more than ready to handle every ounce of pressure the Chargers sent on Sunday, and it was beyond frustrating to see over and over again. It was like I was watching in slow motion as a defender would sprint out of his hole to chase a pass-catcher, only for a Cardinal to immediately replace him and catch a short pass with space to run. All game long it was this way. And not to mention how utterly unstoppable Trey McBride looked. I get it, he’s really good and probably the league’s best tight end, but the Chargers looked like little kids trying to stop him. It seriously reminded me of the way Travis Kelce tore us up in his prime. O’Leary may honestly just need to settle his unit down and give it another go. It was, after all, his first NFL game calling a defense. I hope he just needs to shake it now that he’s gotten his feet wet. Q: On a similar note, the Chargers seemingly had no answer for Cardinals tight end Trey McBride, who had nine catches for 95 yards and a touchdown last week. If he’s healthy, I’d imagine Klint Kubiak is going to try to mimic Arizona’s game plan with Brock Bowers. So, how did McBride have success in Los Angeles last week? A: McBride was used right out of the gate against the Cardinals as he began the game with a big catch up the seam. From there, Arizona utilized him in a ton of triangle reads where he was either the bait to move defenders or as the primary receiver in the route concept. When the defense was stuck on McBride, Kendrick Bourne or Michael Wilson got to benefit. When Bourne or Wilson started slicing them up, Brissett went back to targeting McBride. Heck, on the only pass…

title: Raiders Mailbag: Will Rob Leonard dial up more blitzes in Las Vegas’ Week 2 matchup against Los Angeles Chargers?
summary: The 24-hour rule has long passed, meaning it’s time to put the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins behind us and start focusing on the Week 2 matchup against a familiar AFC West foe: the Los Angeles Chargers. To help preview the game, let’s get into this week’s mailbag! Q: Do […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 24-hour rule has long passed, meaning it’s time to put the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins behind us and start focusing on the Week 2 matchup against a familiar AFC West foe: the Los Angeles Chargers . To help preview the game, let’s get into this week’s mailbag! Q: Do you think Rob Leonard dials up the pressure this week and goes after the Chargers’ IOL? O/U 45% blitz rate for this one? A: I’ll take the under on 45 percent because only two teams — the Vikings (mad man Brian Flores at over 80%) and Commanders (50.9%) — were above that mark in Week 1, according to Ryan Paganetti on X/Twitter . Granted, the Jets (44.9%), Ravens (43.4%) and Lions (43.0%) were pretty close to the number. Meanwhile, the Raiders blitzed just 24.0% of the time against Miami, which ranked 18th across the league. Could Leonard dial up the heat more in Los Angeles? Sure, and I think you’re onto something about the Chargers’ interior offensive line, which is the weakest part of their roster. With free-agent signing Tyler Biadasz out for the year, they have a rookie center in Jake Slaughter, meaning the Bolts have a young lineman making his second NFL start in the position that typically helps set the protection scheme. Having a veteran quarterback like Justin Herbert helps with that, but the Shanahan coaching tree (which L.A.’s new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel is a branch of) typically likes to have the center set the protection to take that off the quarterback’s plate. It sounds like McDaniel has adjusted with Biadasz’s injury, since Jim Harbaugh said this week that Herbert calls the team’s protections (h/t ESPN’s Kris Rhim ). But it’s still a new offense that doesn’t have a veteran center as a fail-safe if things aren’t going well. Circling back to the question, given the Chargers’ weakness up front, I think it’s safe to assume Leonard will at least give them a variety of looks at the beginning of the game and adjust later on if needed. However, I wouldn’t be surprised if the actual blitz rate (rushing five or more defenders) stays pretty consistent. Instead, I’d expect to see more simulated pressures where the Raiders give a blitz look pre-snap and have an off-ball linebacker (Quay Walker or Nakobe Dean) rush the passer while a lineman (Malcolm Koonce, Kwity Paye or one of the defensive tackles) drops into a zone coverage. Or creeper blitzes, which are the same concept of rushing a typical coverage defender and having a typical pass rusher drop into coverage; it just doesn’t present a blitz look pre-snap. That was primarily how Leonard manufactured pressure in Week 1, and is a good way to keep a young or bad offensive line guessing. It makes it more difficult for the line to know where the pass-rush is coming from and can lead to missed communictions/assignments and free rushers for the defense. That’s where not having a veteran center can really hurt because they have more experience to point out potential blitz or pass-rush threats pre-snap, versus a rookie who is just trying to not screw up the snap count. Q: The defense performed better than expected, granted it was against Miami. Do you think it has potential to be a top 15 defense this year? A: If you had asked me this a week ago, I would have said no chance after watching how they struggled to stop the run during the preseason. However, I was very impressed by Leonard’s scheme and have a lot more confidence that the defense can put up league-average numbers this year. There’s definitely the potential to get up to being a Top 15 unit if they continue to play like they did last Sunday. But to pour some cold water on the hot Raiders’ defense, I don’t want to overreact to a performance against a team competing for the No. 1 pick. So, this week — and really the next three games with the Chargers, Saints and Chiefs on the upcoming schedule — will be a better indicator for how good Las Vegas’ defense really is. If the unit continues to look strong down that stretch, now we’re cooking with gasoline! Q: Week 1 Fact or Fiction: This Raiders team is well coached and well schemed and could be looking at .500 or better this year? Or the flip-side version: all they did was beat the Dolphins, and Miami is so bad it’s going to make our players and scheme look great? Kwity Paye/Treydan Stukes are going to be fringe Pro Bowlers? A: The first bullet is the million-dollar question right now that we’ll have a better answer to after Sunday. There’s no doubt that the schedule makers threw Vegas a bone with the Week 1 matchup against Miami, and the Dolphins’ roster is so young that it can give a false sense of hope for the Raiders moving forward. However, I was very impressed with Kubiak’s and Leonard’s play calling in Week 1. Kubiak did an excellent job of finding creative ways to get Ashton Jeanty the ball, which was huge with Brock Bowers out and a cast of wide receivers that even the coach has admitted leaves something to be desired. Also, he did an excellent job with his 21 personnel packages , which again, is especially impressive without the team’s best tight end. Defensively, Leonard had all three levels constantly moving and, in addition to what was said above about manufacturing pressure, had a good scheme to get Maxx Crosby one-on-one matchups. My tone on the Tape Don’t Lie film review conveyed this: I haven’t been this excited about a defensive scheme from the Raiders in years. A good scheme can translate from week to week and help overcome a talent gap. However, there are plenty of good coaches in the NFL, and it is still a talent-driven league. But I definitely think there is more reason to be optimistic about the Raiders moving forward, and that they can win more games than originally expected. Paye and Stukes played pretty well last week, but calling them fringe Pro Bowlers would be a stretch at this point. While he had eight pressures and two sacks in the opener, Paye is still a complementary rusher. He doesn’t get a lot of quick wins, and his best trait is having a high motor. Those types of players are valuable to a defense because they can come up with clean-up sacks, where the coverage is holding up or another rusher wins but misses the tackle. That’s the difference between a quarterback extending the play and beating the defense on scrambles versus a drive-killing loss of yards. However, that’s not exactly a Pro Bowl-caliber type of player since Paye’s production is reliant on his teammates. As for Stukes, he had the interception and a handful of impressive reps mixed in during his NFL debut. But he also had a few “rookie moments” with a missed assignment, a missed tackle and a play in coverage where he looked up for the ball late, resulting in a first-down catch. Don’t get me wrong, I was very encouraged with how the rookie played, especially considering it was his first start at a new position. However, let’s pump the brakes a bit and let him play a few more games before we start throwing around the postseason accolades. Q: How much will the Chargers miss Jesse Minter this year? A: If the season opener was any indication, a lot! Los Angeles gave up 393 yards to Arizona last week , which would have been the second-most its defense allowed all of last season. What’s even more surprising is the Cardinals were viewed in the same category as the Dolphins heading into the season. Maybe that’s a sign Arizona will be better than expected, but the Chargers also had a lot of missed assignments or moments where their defense wasn’t on the same page. That indicates the players aren’t comfortable with the scheme yet, and that’s surprising because the reason Harbaugh hired Chris O’Leary as defensive coordinator is that O’Leary was on the staff as the safeties coach under Minter in 2024. Presumably, that should mean the scheme is pretty similar to what the players are used to. I can’t say I’ve really dived into the differences between the…

title: Raiders’ defense is key against  Chargers’ offense
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders week 2 opponents are the hated rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers. Making a short-distance first road trip to the Raiders’ second home stadium, SoFi Stadium. Taking on a Jim Harbaugh-led team with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel as both the play designer and play caller. McDaniel is coming off being fired as […]
full_text: (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders week 2 opponents are the hated rivals, the Los Angeles Chargers. Making a short-distance first road trip to the Raiders’ second home stadium, SoFi Stadium. Taking on a Jim Harbaugh-led team with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel as both the play designer and play caller. McDaniel is coming off being fired as the Miami Dolphins’ head coach for a lack of wins and offensive inefficiency. Coming off a 26-14 loss to the Arizona Cardinals, the Chargers have more questions than answers. “The league’s best quarterback, Justin Herbert,” threw for 209 yards, a touchdown, and an interception. Top rusher Omarion Hampton had 12 carries for 43 yards and a touchdown, proving the rushing attack wasn’t anything special against the Cardinals’ defense. Ladd McConkey’s five catches for 82 yards and a touchdown was the featured pass catcher of the day. For the first half of the game it was pure gimmick offense. Smoke screens, motions, pure gimmicks, no substance, and no run game. When the Chargers had to play from behind that Mike McDaniel offense looked like it’s always been, two cans of shark shit. https://t.co/47oAxf393n — Breiden Fehoko (@BreidenFehoko) September 13, 2026 Fehoko, is a former Chargers nose tackle who played against McDaniel’s offense and dominated it. As amusing as it may be to watch Chargers on Chargers crime, the great French general, Napoleon Bonaparte, once said: “Never interrupt your enemy when they are making a mistake.” Harbaugh has admitted that he didn’t give his starters enough preseason action and it showed against the Cardinals in a lack of physicality. Completely unheard of for a Harbaugh-coached team. What does it mean for the Raiders defense? Folorunso Fatukasi, Adam Butler, “Professional game-wrecker” Maxx Crosby and Kwity Paye will face both an embarrassed coaching staff and an embarrassed offensive line. McDaniel and Harbaugh will most likely view the undersized defensive line as an opportunity to run 12/13 personnel (one running back and two/three tight ends) and attack them with power football. Misdirection and attacking the backside of the field is where the Chargers had the largest impact against the Cardinals. Featuring a mixture of run-pass options, play-action passes, gun runs and in-breaking routes were hallmarks of McDaniel’s offense. However, the offensive line wasn’t sharp, allowing lots of pressure on Herbert and forcing him to alter his launch points quite frequently. Raiders second-year cornerback Darian Porter will miss the game against the Chargers and either Hezekiah Masses or Jermod McCoy will have to be the next man up. McConkey is listed as questionable and his absence would be a further detriment to the offense. Should he play, will Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard allow his number one cornerback, Eric Stokes, to travel with McConkey on both sides of the field? Final thoughts: The Chargers offense represents a step up, talent-wise, from the Miami Dolphins. Hampton is a one-cut runner without much wiggle or shimmy, yet still capable of breaking tackles if allowed to gain a head of steam. Should Fatukasi continue getting a great jump into the backfield on both run and pass plays the defense will be in good shape. Remember the Chargers offensive line had a huge problem picking up twists, stunts and blitzes. Against the Dolphins the Raiders tallied five sacks doing just that.

title: Miami Dolphins review: 5 Things I Think I Think About Week 1
summary: Did Week 1 go as well as I had hoped? Am I optimistic about the Miami Dolphins’ chances in Week 2 against the 49ers? Are the Dolphins going to go 0-17? I say: No, no and gosh I hope not. Here are five things I think I think about the Dolphins after their disappointing Week […]
full_text: Did Week 1 go as well as I had hoped? Am I optimistic about the Miami Dolphins’ chances in Week 2 against the 49ers? Are the Dolphins going to go 0-17? I say: No, no and gosh I hope not. Here are five things I think I think about the Dolphins after their disappointing Week 1 loss to the Raiders. The future showed up early. OK, so we know this is a young team. As Marek pointed out a few weeks ago , the average age of the Dolphins 53-man roster (as of 8/31) is 25.3 years, easily the youngest in the league. You’d expect a massive learning curve with all that youth – yet, by and large, the rookies held their own. Caleb Douglas caught 5 of 7 targets for 94 yards and proved to be physical, polished and an accomplished run blocker. Jacob Rodriguez’s 14 tackles were the most from a Dolphins rookie since Zach Thomas’ 16 in 1996. (Here, go take a look .) Chris Johnson had 11 tackles and 2 passes defensed. Rookie Michael Taaffe and second-year safety Dante Trader each had picks. (Trader was PFF’s top-rated Dolphin, with a 91.8 defensive grade that was two points higher than Jordyn Brooks’.) Was it perfect? It was not. But if this is the baseline for what we can expect going forward, it’s hard not to be excited. Our trench play has to get better. Simply put, we were manhandled on both sides of the line of scrimmage. Offensively, we struggled to establish the run – Achane finished the game with only 11 carries for 36 yards – and Malik Willis was sacked 5 times. Defensively, we could not get any pressure on Raiders QB Kirk Cousins, who is 85 years old and needs a walker to cross the street. It wasn’t just the zero (!) sacks – Chop Robinson finished the game with exactly 1 tackle. By comparison, Riley Patterson had 2 tackles for the game, and he’s the kicker. The kicker! Maybe we should put him on the defensive line! To be fair, Robinson might have suffered a concussion during the game. Regardless, Jeff Hafley’s defenses have historically been good at stopping the run and forcing opponents into uncomfortable down-and-distance situations. Against the Raiders, Cousins and company had little trouble moving the ball. Malik Willis was better than the box score. With all the money Willis received in the offseason to be our starting quarterback, it’s easy to forget that he entered the season with only 155 career passes under his belt. While he had some impressive game tape from his time in Green Bay, much of that was against defenses that had prepared all week for Jordan Love. The big question entering Week 1 was what Willis would look like with an offense built around him. All in all, I think he acquitted himself reasonably well. He made some strong, NFL-caliber throws, especially downfield near the sidelines. He also showed good processing and was able to make things happen with his legs (including a TD run). There were problem too: He held the ball for longer than 3 seconds on average, which was a major reason behind his five sacks. He also missed some easy throws and seemed to press on the interception. Still, there’s a lot to build on. The coaches need to prove themselves as much as the players. I have a lot of faith in Coach Hafley – already I think we’ve shown more heart and discipline than the team did at any point with Mike McDaniel, and the fact that we actually won a challenge makes me feel we’re playing with house money. Offensively, I’m not sure we were prepared with the right game plan for the Raiders, one of the easiest teams we’ll face this year. We had runs and deep balls, but not much in between to keep the pass rush at bay. And our special teams were anything but special – it felt like the Raiders were starting each drive at midfield throughout the game. To be sure, it was only one game, and when you’re starting so many first- and second-year players, it’s not always going to look pretty. Still, it’s something to keep an eye on. This team is better than the score might suggest. Although any loss is disappointing – and especially to a team that is decidedly beatable – we weren’t outclassed despite our youth. Look at how many plays the team left on the field: For as impressive a debut as he had, Caleb Douglas had opportunities for an even bigger afternoon. Malik Willis narrowly missed several explosive plays. There were scramble-drill opportunities that never connected because Willis and his receivers weren’t on the same page. A tipped pass late could have been a touchdown. Several defensive busts were one assignment away from becoming stops. The Dolphins were often a step late, a yard short or a read away from turning negative plays into game-changing ones. You don’t get consolation prizes for losing, but on a rebuilding team, there’s a lot to work with here. The good news? Many of the Dolphins’ mistakes looked like inexperience rather than a lack of talent, which means they should be correctable in time. The bad news? The 49ers won’t be nearly as forgiving as the Raiders. Let’s see how much this young team learned from Week 1.

title: Dolphins fan confidence dips, concerns mount heading into Week 2 vs. 49ers
summary: The Miami Dolphins struggled in all three aspects of their game against the Las Vegas Raiders, faltering on offense, laboring on defense, and getting gashed by long special-teams returns. It was not an ideal start to the season. This season is not about wins and losses, though. This year’s focus is on the team developing […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NV - SEPTEMBER 13: Miami Dolphins linebacker Chop Robinson (44) walks off of the field after a NFL regular season game between the Las Vegas Raiders and Miami Dolphins at Allegiant Stadium, Sunday September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, NV. (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins struggled in all three aspects of their game against the Las Vegas Raiders, faltering on offense, laboring on defense, and getting gashed by long special-teams returns. It was not an ideal start to the season. This season is not about wins and losses, though. This year’s focus is on the team developing the younger players and building toward the future. Miami is rebuilding, turning over much of the roster as a new front office and coaching staff put their stamp on the team. Things may not get better this week as the Dolphins visit the San Francisco 49ers. According to the latest FanDuel Sportsbook odds , the Dolphins are 13.5-point underdogs. Not a lot is expected of Miami later today. Fans concerned about lack of pass rush The Raiders’ offensive line struggled to protect the quarterback in 2025. Last week, Miami could not get near Kirk Cousins. The pass rush simply never materialized. Now, the fans see it as the biggest area of concern with the team. Out SB Nation Reacts poll for this week asked for where the concerns were for the Dolphins moving forward, and the fans zeroed in on the pass rush – and this is before the team’s top rusher, Chop Robinson, was ruled out of today’s game with a concussion – with 42 percent of the responses expecting more from the group. The offensive line received 20 percent of the votes, special teams 13 percent, and the cornerbacks 4 percent. The remaining 22 percent voted “other.” Discussion around the poll included concerns about offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik, penalties, and fans turning on the team and not giving the rebuild the time it needs to turn the franchise around. Dolphins fan confidence The Dolphins’ struggles against the Raiders were not unexpected, but it was still a rough game to watch. Our weekly fan confidence poll reflects the fan conflict between wanting to watch a competitive team putting up wins and the understanding that the team is resetting this year and building for the future. Last week, 79 percent of the fan base said they were positive about the team’s direction. With the loss to the Raiders now on the board, our fan confidence poll dipped, but maybe not as much as a loss like that would have last year. According to our Week 2 survey, 63 percent of the fans are still supportive of the direction Miami is taking. Miami Dolphins 2026 Season Fan Confidence Results: Preseason – 80% Week 1 – 79% Week 2 – 63% National Poll: Worst quarterback situation in league This week’s SB Nation Reacts National survey included a question about the worst quarterback situations in the league. The Dolphins showed up in the results, but were nowhere near the top. Miami received six percent of the vote, more than the Minnesota Vikings (five percent) and the New England Patriots (two percent). The Cleveland Browns dominated the results, receiving 67 percent of the vote. DeShaun Watson is starting for Cleveland, though he does not look comfortable, with Shedeur Sanders and Taylen Green backing him up. Dillon Gabriel is on injured reserve. The Atlanta Falcons, who have a quarterback room that includes former Dolphins starting quarterback Tua Tagovailoa along with Michael Penix, Jr., Cooper Rush, and Nick Muse, picked up 19 percent of the votes, landing them in second place. Tagovailoa was expected to start the season at the top of the depth chart, but he missed the opener with an oblique injury and is doubtful for today. Do you agree with the Dolphins’ fan confidence poll results? What is the biggest area of concern for the team? Let us know in the comments.

Mandatory Credit: David Brytus-Imagn Images. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Miami Dolphins are into their final preparations for their Week 2 game against the San Francisco 49ers, but there is still some discussion about the team’s Week 1 game against the Las Vegas Raiders. To be more specific, the talk is about gloves used in the Week 1 game. Miami center Aaron Brewer wore orange gloves as the team faced an opponent wearing black jerseys. Brewer was flagged for holding during the game, with former NFL center Mark Schlereth, now a FOX broadcaster, placing some of the blame for the penalty on Brewer’s gloves. Schlereth said that if he were a Dolphins coach, he would make Brewer change to black gloves, allowing his hands to blend into the Raiders’ jersey. South Florida Sun Sentinel reporter David Furones looked into the NFL’s equipment rules and discussed the situation: League rules limit the colors players can use on certain equipment, like gloves and cleats. They can only wear white, black or team-colored gloves, so aqua and orange are added to the list for Dolphins players. For Sunday’s game against the 49ers, Miami already announced it will wear white jerseys. That could mean the 49ers wear scarlet. Those same orange gloves could work for Brewer — with orange not far from the dark red — or just black gloves. Schlereth, a former Pro Bowl guard, did not agree with the penalty in general, as Brewer was grabbing Raiders defensive tackle Folorunso Fatukasi’s jersey in the chest area. “For me, that’s one of those situations, an inside grab on the chest plate of the defender, that should never be called holding, ever,” Schlereth said. “But again, I’d still go get them damn orange gloves off.” Check out that story, and a complete collection of recent Dolphins news below as you enter the Splash Zone: Did glove color contribute to a holding call against Dolphins’ Aaron Brewer? – David Furones, South Florida Sun Sentinel When Miami Dolphins center Aaron Brewer had a holding penalty called against him in last Sunday’s season-opening loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, a big deal was made on the Fox broadcast over Brewer wearing orange gloves. title: Dolphins vs 49ers predictions, prop bets, and odds in Week 2
summary: The Miami Dolphins’ Week 1 performance left much to be desired as they lost 27-13 to the Las Vegas Raiders. They face a tough test in Week 2 against the San Francisco 49ers as they hope to rebound. The Dolphins are young, unproven, and still growing together as a team. Will a week of being […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 13: De'von Achane #28 of the Miami Dolphins runs the ball in the second quarter of a game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins’ Week 1 performance left much to be desired as they lost 27-13 to the Las Vegas Raiders. They face a tough test in Week 2 against the San Francisco 49ers as they hope to rebound. The Dolphins are young, unproven, and still growing together as a team. Will a week of being together in California, staying out west between the two road games rather than returning to Florida, allow the team to develop a better chemistry and lead to better execution? Predictions for the Dolphins’ 2026 season have only worsened after Week 1’s performance. Miami seems like a lock for the first-overall pick, with the possibility of an 0-17 season growing, at least according to the analysts. The 49ers, meanwhile, are considered a top-ten team in the league, one which should be eyeing a deep run the postseason. Two teams on opposite ends of the spectrum meet in Santa Clara tomorrow, and Miami does not look like it has much of a chance, at least according to the latest odds. Here are some predictions for Sunday’s game: All odds provides by FanDuel Sportsbook . Dolphins (+13.5) at 49ers Last week, I thought Miami could pull off the upset and leave Las Vegas with a victory. This week, I just want them to stay competitive. This does not look like a great day for the team or the fans. San Francisco is the better team and should be able to prove it early. Can the Dolphins keep it close? They will have to play better in all three phases of the game (especially on special teams) if they want to at least stay within the point spread – the only double-digit spread in the league this week. Assuming Miami realizes they have to get running back De’Von Achane more involved than he was last week (11 carries, 36 yards, 4 receptions, 30 yards), the offense should have a little better day this week. The Dolphins’ goal for this year is to get better each week – hopefully that happens. I will take the points to cover for Miami, but the 49ers should win straight up. Prop Bets Malik Willis passing yards: 183.5 Over: -114 Under: -114 Willis threw for 220 yards last week and, given Miami will likely be playing from behind for much of this game, he should have a similar total this week. The Dolphins know they have to get Achane involved more than they did last week, but that could include using him as a receiving option as they try to stay within striking distance. I will take the over. De’Von Achane rushing & receiving yards: 90.5 Over : -115 Under: -113 Achane must be the focal point of the Dolphins’ offense, and they have to get him touches. I like this prop better than Achane’s 58.5 rushing yards line because I think Miami may have to lean more on the passing game than they would like. Achane could get heavy usage as a receiver out of the backfield and in the slot. I will take the over because Achane should top 100 yards if Miami has a chance in this game. Greg Dulcich receptions: 2.5 Over: +134 Under: -180 The spotlight for the passing game last week was on rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas, who blew past the 2.5-reception line set for him, catching five passes for 94 yards (and, of course, I thought he would have a quiet first game, hitting the under). Tight end Greg Dulcich caught two passes for 18 yards against the Raiders. Again, I think the Dolphins will have to pass the ball to stay with the 49ers, which should lead to plenty of targets for all of Miami’s receiving options. I will go with the over here with Willis using Dulcich as a check-down option. Zach Sieler records a sack Record a sack : +148 I do not recommend this prop. The Dolphins need a big performance from Sieler, especially since edge rusher Chop Robinson has been ruled out , but the veteran has not been as impactful recently as he was in the past. It used to seem like whenever Miami needed a play, Sieler was there to make it. Now, Sieler seems to have lost a step. He can still make an impact, but it is hard to predict that, yes, he will record a sack.

(Photo by Aric Becker/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images Week 3 of the college football schedule features a massive contest between two top-10-ranked teams: (7) LSU at (8) Ole Miss. This matchup pits two top-10 teams against each other in an SEC rivalry game, and it features head coach Lane Kiffin, who left Ole Miss in 2025 for the LSU job. This game will have a huge draw tonight when they kickoff at 7:30 p.m. Eastern. Will you be watching the game? Would you like to know some potential Miami Dolphins draft prospects to watch during the game? We have you covered. Here are five players from each team to watch tonight: LSU 2027 Draft prospects Sam Leavitt, quarterback (Redshirt Junior) – Why not start at the quarterback position? Leavitt joins LSU to continue his college career after starting at Michigan State in 2023, then playing at Arizona State in 2024 and 2025. He is likely a late day-two prospect, but could improve his draft stock under Kiffin. He has a strong arm and can get outside the pocket to keep plays alive, but he is not a typical pocket-passing quarterback and needs to improve his reads. He is probably a backup quarterback at the NFL level, but could be an interesting development project behind Malik Willis if the Dolphins are not looking for a starter in the 2027 Draft. Jordan Seaton, tackle (Junior) – Seaton transferred to LSU this year after two seasons at Colorado. He projects as a potential top-ten pick, so he may not be available unless the Dolphins are using their first pick on him – and they would have to be in desperate need at tackle for that to be the case. Patrick Paul appears set at left tackle, while Austin Jackson is a good right tackle if he stays healthy, and guard Kadyn Proctor could move out to tackle if needed. Tackle does not seem like an area Miami could address with their first pick, but if Seaton is the selection, they could add another cornerstone to the rebuild. He has exceptional footwork, and he knows how to move around in his space. He is stronger in pass protection than in run blocking right now, but he can develop that. If Miami is ready to move on from Jackson and they believe Willis is their quarterback, Seaton could be a major option for Miami. Trey’Dez Green, tight end (Junior) – Greg Dulcich is a solid starter for the Dolphins this year, but he only has a one-year contract, and the team could look for a dynamic option to upgrade the position next year. A 6-foot-7 freak of an athlete, Green can be a pass-catching machine. He had only 33 receptions last year, but in two games this season, he already has 10 receptions for 162 yards and a touchdown. He is a huge red-zone target and can attack the seams. He feels like Mike Gesicki to some degree – he has to add to his blocking ability to become a true tight end and be more than just a receiving option, but he has a huge upside in the passing game right now. If he proves he can block, the Dolphins could be interested, though he could go off the board too early for Miami to consider the position. Jordan Ross, edge (Junior) – A Tennessee transfer, Ross could factor into the Dolphins’ day-two plans. Head coach Jeff Hafley is defensive-minded and always looks to add new edge rushers. Ross has a great first step and uses his speed to get after the quarterback. He needs to continue to develop his pass rush options, and he has to prove he can shed blocks in to stop the run, but he has a ton of potential that Hafley could covet. Braelin Moore, center (Redshirt Senior) – After three years at Virginia Tech, Moore is now in his second season at LSU. He has been a starter for most of his college careerand will bring plenty of experience to the NFL. He began as a guard at Virginia Tech before moving to center and could be asked to play either role professionally. He may not have the size to best fit as a center and hold up against NFL defensive tackles, but he is disciplined and is not afraid to get physical. He could be a day-three backup option for Miami behind Aaron Brewer. Ole Miss 2027 Draft prospects Trinidad Chambliss, quarterback (Redshirt Senior) – We started at quarterback for LSU, so we will do the same for Ole Miss. Chambliss is probably a second-round pick; he has upside that could be developed. He might be a perfect fit as the backup to Malik Willis, playing with a similar style. He has a strong arm and he runs really well. He has not proven he can be a drop-back quarterback, but he has the raw tools to succeed. He finished eighth in the Heisman Trophy voting last year after throwing for 3,937 yards with 22 touchdowns and three interceptions, along with 527 rushing yards and eight touchdowns. Clearly a developmental, backup candidate, Chambliss would be an interesting addition if he can continue to develop. Will Echoles, defensive tackle (Junior) – Echoles explodes off the line at the snap, pushing linemen back into the pocket and creating confusion. He is clearly a power rusher who needs to add options to turn into an effective NFL pass-rushing defensive tackle, but as a run stuffer who can eat up blocks, Echoles excels. Echoles could continue Miami’s desire to build from the inside out, though the developing young players, including Kenneth Grant, Jordan Phillips, and Zeek Biggers, all of whom were 2025 draft picks, might keep Miami from heavily targeting the interior defensive line in 2027. Needing development, Echoles could land anywhere from early in the first round to sometime in the second. Suntarine Perkins, linebacker/edge (Senior) – Perkins could land anywhere in the draft order at this point, from the second through the fifth round. He has spent most of his college career as an edge-rushing linebacker, but he probably projects better as a coverage, weakside linebacker in the NFL. His draft position may depend on a coaching staff and front office weighing his athleticism and potential more than what he shows on game tape. He has the speed to work sideline-to-sideline and he can chase down the ball. If he can prove he has coverage skills, he could be a perfect multi-role player for Hafley’s defense. Kam Franklin, edge (Junior) – Franklin is probably a day-two or day-three prospect who could even slide into the end of the first round with a strong season. He may have to slide inside in the NFL if his pass-rush skills do not develop this season, but he is exceptional at setting the edge and getting after the run. A pure power rusher, Franklin disrupts the pocket more by shoving linemen backward than by threatening the quarterback with pass-rush moves. Right now, he is most likely a rotational piece on run downs. Antonio Kite, cornerback (Redshirt Junior) – Kite is a late-round or undrafted free agent target. He began his college career at Alabama, but saw minimal playing time. He then transferred to Auburn after two seasons, but academic issues in 2025 led him to transfer to Ole Miss after just one season there. He saw his most playing time in 2025, playing in 12 games with 34 tackles and five passes defensed. He only has one career interception. He is an undersized cornerback (6-foot, 180 pounds) who may be pigeonholed as a slot corner at the NFL level and likely needs a zone-heavy defensive scheme. He is not a sure tackler and provides little run support. Special teams may be his best path to an NFL roster.
author: Kevin Nogle

title: Miami Dolphins Week 2: What they said
summary: The Miami Dolphins face the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, hoping to bounce back in Week 2 after a less-than-stellar Week 1 performance against the Las Vegas Raiders. Miami will be without their top edge rusher as Chop Robinson has been ruled out of the game, making an already tough game even more difficult. What […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 21: Chop Robinson #44 of the Miami Dolphins plays against the Cincinnati Bengals during the second half of the game at Hard Rock Stadium on December 21, 2025 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins face the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, hoping to bounce back in Week 2 after a less-than-stellar Week 1 performance against the Las Vegas Raiders. Miami will be without their top edge rusher as Chop Robinson has been ruled out of the game , making an already tough game even more difficult. What did the Dolphins players and coaches say about their preparations for the 49ers? We break down what they said throughout the week. Chop Robinson’s injury Head coach Jeff Hafley: “Everyone’s going to ask me about Chop, so I’ll just jump right into that. Chop did sustain a concussion during practice; he is in the protocol. He will not play this week. He is doing well and I will leave it at that for Chop questions as that one goes.” Jeff Hafley on how to replace Robinson and if edge rushers Malik Herring and Clelin Ferrell factor into the plan: “It’s all of the above and we might do some other things to help out. But those guys, I have confidence in. They’ve been getting better. They all haven’t been here for the entire time, but they’ve done a nice job in practice this week and it’ll be the next man up.” Defensive coordinator Sean Duggan on preparing to use other edge rushers: “I think your job as a coach is to prepare everybody, right? I mean, you never know what could happen, it’s an unpredictable game. So we should always have the mindset that we’re trying to get everybody ready to play.” Other injury updates Jeff Hafley on long snapper Tucker Addington’s status: “We’ll see how Tucker goes today and how he feels. We have 48 hours to the game, so hopefully he’ll feel good enough to snap for us on Sunday.” Jeff Hafley on tight end Syedou Traore’s status: “Traore will practice today. So again, we’ll see how it goes, but I would anticipate him being out there today at practice. I would anticipate – we’ll see what happens today, but I would anticipate him being out there on Sunday unless there’s some setbacks.” Special Teams coordinator Chris Tabor on replacing Kyle Louis as a primary gunner on punt coverage: “I think we’re still working all through that. I think that it is next man up. We’re going to see who the next man up is and then see what kind of production we can get from there.” Improving after Raiders game in Week 1 Sean Duggan on corrections the edge rushers can make: “I think the thing we’re talking to our guys a lot about is I felt like we kind of tiptoed a little bit early, especially early in the game. I think they got comfortable as the game went on and our play got better. What I really want to see is guys go play confident, cut it loose a little bit, but within the realm of our defense and within having great fundamentals. I think you can see the physicality and our ability. We can stop the run. We can rush and affect the quarterback. I know, the numbers are what they were, but Kirk was doing a really good job getting the ball out of his hand. But I think affecting the quarterback is more than just stats. It’s closing the pocket, it’s affecting throws, which I think we did, particularly in the second half. I really just want to see us continue to build on that.” Defensive tackle Zach Sieler on improving the run defense in the second half: “You know, we just kind of settled down, made the right adjustments, started seeing the game as one and kind of was able to take a breath in the halftime and make the right adjustments, like I said. I think we were able to kind of get out there and really put our foot in the right direction.” Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik on quarterback Malik Willis’s performance: “Yeah, I thought really what we set out to do in the game was we wanted to make sure we went out, we competed, we fought, and we emphasized the style of play we wanted to have. I thought by and large we accomplished that. We need to clean up the football a lot. I thought the execution for us really wasn’t there at the clip we wanted to be at. I mean, we had a lot of mistakes through the course of the game. Now we have a lot of young guys playing, we got a lot of new guys to the scheme and the system and what we’re trying to do. I think we’re all trying to learn and figure each other out through this process. So there’s going to be a process to that early in the year, but we know the urgency we need to have to get better and for our young guys to grow and grow fast. And that’s really where we’re at right now.” Bobby Slowik on allowing five sacks and if there were cases when Willis needed to get rid of the ball: “There’s usually a little bit of everything when you exit a game with multiple sacks or a handful of sacks. It’s typically a combination of maybe a poor play call on my part, poor protection up front, or the ball should have been gone and it’s not, or someone messed up on a route so we can’t get the ball out where we need to get it out to. And I would say on all five of those, and even some other situations in the past game where they were close to being sacks, it was multiple factors on all of them. Like consistently through the game for us, run game, pass game, as far as protection, throwing the ball, run IDs, getting connected and doing our assignment in the run game to give De’Von windows, like there was just multiple execution breakdowns that we know we need to clean up. That’s the emphasis for us this week.” Center Aaron Brewer on how the offensive line could have played better: “I’d say in all areas, it wasn’t a perfect game as we’ve seen. We had some good pockets and we held up for a while and also it was some that collapsed faster than we wanted it to. So in those areas could have been better. Run game, we had a couple opportunities. I think we ran it with probably 10, 11 times and in those times most of our runs was positive. We gained at least two, three-plus yards every run. In those that was pretty good as well, but we also need to be better. We didn’t score enough points. In those areas, we need to do better.” Quarterback Malik Willis on quarterbacks keeping an internal clock to avoid pass rush: “No, I feel like that’s made up. There’s no such thing as a clock, there’s just what it is. I mean, sometimes they win fast, sometimes they win slow, it’s just understanding the feel of when are they going to get there more than a clock telling you, ‘okay, I need to throw it now.‘ Cause that’s bad ball if you’re working off of that. You got to see what’s going on out in the coverage and how that plays out. Maybe somebody got rerouted. It’s a lot of different stuff. I wouldn’t say I have a longer clock or not. I try to trust my guys to get open and our o-line to do a great job as they have been.“ Bobby Slowik on Willis’ comments about the internal clock: “I think the longer I’m around the game and offensive football, the more I think there’s so many different ways to play the position. Jimmy (Garoppolo) played it different than Brock (Purdy) played it different than when I was with C.J. (Stroud) and Davis Mills and they played different than Malik Willis and last year when I was here with Tua and Quinn. They all have like these little different ways of what fits them. I think the way Malik verbalized that is that’s very much how he plays the game. And what he’s focusing on right now is like, OK, when the play presents itself the way we want it to present itself, can I take advantage of it? Get the ball out to the guy we want to get the ball out to, and then that will take care of the internal clock on its own. But right now, particularly up front, like our o-line guys know what he can do. And they know how talented he is as a runner and how talented he is off schedule. So we’re trying like heck to make sure we’re straining to block and block longer.…
author: Kevin Nogle

title: Dolphins’ Chop Robinson out for Sunday vs. 49ers
summary: After being downgraded on Thursday’s injury report following a concussion, Dolphins’ edge rusher Chop Robinson has officially been ruled out ahead of Sunday afternoon’s game against the San Francisco 49ers. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said Robinson suffered the concussion during Wednesday’s practice. It is Robinson’s third concussion within the last year. Also ruled out of the game […]
full_text: After being downgraded on Thursday’s injury report following a concussion, Dolphins’ edge rusher Chop Robinson has officially been ruled ou t ahead of Sunday afternoon’s game against the San Francisco 49ers. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said Robinson suffered the concussion during Wednesday’s practice. It is Robinson’s third concussion within the last year. Also ruled out of the game was linebacker Ronnie Harrison, Jr. Primarily a special teams player in Week 1, Harrison has been dealing with a hamstring injury that kept him from practicing all week. With Robinson sidelined, Josh Uche, Malik Herring, Robert Beal Jr., and potentially Clelin Ferrell, who is currently on the practice squad, are all candidates to see increased workloads. Hafley could also continue deploying defensive tackle Zeek Biggers on the edge, as he did during last Sunday’s loss to the Raiders. Miami’s injury report also listed long snapper Tucker Addington as questionable for the game. Addington injured his shoulder in Week 1 but played through the rest of the game. The 49ers’ side of the injury report included officially ruling out wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling who did not practice throughout the week with an ankle injury. as well as designating running back Kaelon Black and kicker Eddy Pineiro as questionable. Black was limited in practice on Thursday and Friday after sustaining a groin injury. Pineiro did not practice all week due to an illness. The Dolphins and 49ers kickoff on Sunday at 4:25 p.m. Eastern.

title: The Wrinkle Game: Why Kevin O’Connell Needs to Get Creative vs. Chicago
summary: Vikings vs. Bears Week 2 preview: Kevon O’Connell doesn’t need a new identity. He needs a wrinkle. Brian Flores trusts rookies, Dallas Turner explodes, Mason’s thumb breaks & Wentz starts at Soldier Field. The Minnesota Vikings face the Chicago Bears in a critical NFC North showdown with a backup quarterback, a fractured running back depth […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings looks on before a game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Vikings vs. Bears Week 2 preview: Kevon O’Connell doesn’t need a new identity. He needs a wrinkle. Brian Flores trusts rookies, Dallas Turner explodes, Mason’s thumb breaks & Wentz starts at Soldier Field. The Minnesota Vikings face the Chicago Bears in a critical NFC North showdown with a backup quarterback, a fractured running back depth chart, and a defense that finally showed signs of youth. In this episode of Two Old Bloggers, Darren Campbell and Dave Stefano break down Brian Flores’ evolving trust in rookies, the devastating loss of Jordan Mason to injured reserve, Dallas Turner’s breakout performance, and a comprehensive Week 2 Bears preview with Drew Bunting. Flores played three defensive rookies against Green Bay — Domonique “Big Citrus” Orange (22 snaps), Caleb Banks (16), and Jacob Thomas (10) — marking a philosophical shift for a coordinator long criticized for favoring veterans. “Brian Flores is not going to give him playing time or any rookie playing time or any player playing time that they don’t earn,” Campbell noted, emphasizing that the door is cracking open. The injury news darkens the outlook: Mason’s fractured thumb sidelines him for four games, leaving Aaron Jones Sr. and journeyman DeeJay Dallas to carry the load. “This is a big loss for the Vikings,” Campbell said. Meanwhile, Turner’s nine-pressure, 89.5 PFF-graded performance validated his first-round pedigree. “Sometimes you just need one guy to beat the guy that is trying to block him, and Dallas Turner did that a lot last Sunday,” Campbell added. Drew Bunting delivered a fiery preview, picking the Bears despite wanting a Vikings win. “Kevin O’Connell has to grow a pair and move the ball,” Bunting declared, calling for offensive wrinkles to counter Dennis Allen’s defense. He emphasized turnovers as the ultimate stat: Kevin O’Connell is 36-4 when winning the turnover margin. “If they lose the turnover battle Sunday, they have no chance,” Bunting warned. Key Points: Brian Flores played 3 defensive rookies vs. Green Bay — his most rookie snaps in a meaningful game Jordan Mason (fractured thumb, IR) out 4 games; Aaron Jones and DeeJay Dallas must step up Dallas Turner: 9–10 pressures, 89.5 PFF grade, looking like an elite edge rusher Josh Metellus’ PFF grades declining — 29.6 in Week 1, 55.4 in 2024 — usage change may be the cause Kyler Murray’s concussion sparks dirty-hit debate; Tedy Bruschi called Javon Bullard’s hit “dirty” Drew Bunting picks Bears: Caleb Williams’ advantage over Carson Wentz too large to ignore Drew’s point : this is a “wrinkle game.” Base flare screens and two-yard throws play right into Dennis Allen. Historic example Drew used: 1978 in Dallas. Bud Grant (via Jerry Burns) put Sammy White in the backfield with Foreman and Ricky Young. Never handed it to him. Cowboys linebackers pointed at each other the rest of the afternoon. Vikings won as heavy underdogs. Vikings on a 6-game win streak at Soldier Field — longest ever Turnover battle: Kevin O’Connell is 36-4 when winning or tying turnover margin Weather could factor — 20–30 mph winds, heavy rain expected at Soldier Field Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: This episode has everything a Vikings fan needs before kickoff — film breakdown, stats, hot takes, and Drew Bunting’s unfiltered preview. Two Old Bloggers is your home for Minnesota Vikings analysis, part of the Vikings 1st & SKOL network and the Bleav Podcast Network. Subscribe, rate, and ring the bell so you never miss a show. Fan With Us! We have your Minnesota Vikings talk amongst the Two Old Bloggers , Darren @KickassblogVike , and Dave @Luft_Krigare along with our numbers guy, Drew Bunting. Join the conversation! Fan with us at Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL on the Bleav Network @BleavNetwork . So here’s the question: Can Kevin O’Connell cook up enough wrinkles to out-scheme Ben Johnson (actually DC Dennis Allen), or will the Bears’ offensive firepower be too much for a Wentz-led Vikings offense at Soldier Field?

title: Vikings Elevate Kyle Van Noy, Dillon Bell from Practice Squad
summary: Ahead of their NFC North clash with the Chicago Bears on Sunday, the Minnesota Vikings have announced a pair of practice squad elevations. The team is moving outside linebacker Kyle Van Noy and wide receiver Dillon Bell from the practice squad to the main roster ahead of Sunday’s game at Soldier Field. Much like last […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Dillon Bell #89 of the Minnesota Vikings fields the opening kick against the Baltimore Ravens during the first quarter of the preseason game at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ahead of their NFC North clash with the Chicago Bears on Sunday, the Minnesota Vikings have announced a pair of practice squad elevations. The team is moving outside linebacker Kyle Van Noy and wide receiver Dillon Bell from the practice squad to the main roster ahead of Sunday’s game at Soldier Field. Much like last week, Van Noy’s elevation does not come as any real surprise. He played 25 snaps on defense last week and will likely continue to play a key role as a reserve this week as he continues to get re-acclimated to Brian Flores’ defense. Bell will help add wide receiver depth in the absence of Jauan Jennings, who is not traveling with the team to Chicago this week due to a family issue. He showed some exciting flashes in the preseason and was thought to have an outside shot at making the 53-man roster, but landed on the practice squad instead. With Jennings out, either Tai Felton or Myles Price will serve as WR3 against the Bears. Both of those players logged just three snaps each at wide receiver last Sunday against Green Bay. Players can be elevated to the active roster from the practice squad three times during a season. After that, they must be signed to the active roster if a team wants to use them again. I would assume that Van Noy will be elevated from the practice squad next week as well and will then be signed to the 53-man roster permanently. The team did not move quarterback Max Brosmer to the 53-man roster, either by elevating him from the practice squad or signing him to the 53-man roster earlier in the week. That means that they’ll go into Chicago with two quarterbacks. Carson Wentz will be the starter, and J.J. McCarthy will serve as the backup. Kyler Murray, who has still not fully cleared concussion protocol, has been declared out for this week. Those should be the last of the moves the team will make before Sunday’s game in Chicago. If they do make any more moves, we will bring them to you here as soon as we have them.

(Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images In conjunction with our friends from the FanDuel Sportsbook , it is once again time to take a look at a couple of player prop bets for this Sunday’s game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Chicago Bears and see if we can’t help those of you who choose to add to your excitement. . .or anxiety. . .of the contest by involving money in things. Hopefully I can do a little bit better than I did last week, when I only hit on one out of the three bets that I put out there. I didn’t know that Jauan Jennings wasn’t going to catch any passes at all, let alone not catch the first touchdown. But, again, here’s hoping that this week will end up being better. Here we go. Justin Jefferson Receiving Yardage : Over 79.5 yards (-114) Yeah, I think I’m just going to hit this one every week until he or somebody else gives me a reason not to. I mean, hey. . .I’ve got to give myself one that should be relatively easy, right? Aaron Jones Rushing Yardage : Over 61.5 yards (-114) To Kevin O’Connell’s credit, he did actually stick with the run game when the Vikings were trailing last week against Green Bay. With Jordan Mason out of this one, the focus of the run game this week will be directly on Jones, and I expect him to respond accordingly, particularly if the weather in Chicago makes things a bit soggy, as is being forecast at the present time. The Bears’ defense was decent enough against the run last week against Carolina, but I expect them to have a little more difficulty with the Vikings this week, so I’d take the over on this one. Harrison Smith to Record an Interception : +650 Smith needs one more interception to join the 40-interception, 20-sack club for his career. He would be just the third defensive back in NFL history to do that, along with Charles Woodson and Ronde Barber. (Those two guys were pretty good.) I know that Caleb Williams does a pretty good job of taking care of the football, but Smith is going to get that pick at some point this season, so why not make it Sunday at Soldier Field? After all, we’ve seen a lot of strange things happen at that place, so we could just add one more to the list. Those are the prop bets I’m keeping my eye on for this Sunday, folks. Are there any you’re going to be looking at? Let us know in the comments!

title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Vikings Fans Less Confident Despite Big Win
summary: It’s time to take a look at the results from our SB Nation Reacts poll for this week, so let’s take a look at how Minnesota Vikings fans are feeling about our favorite football team. Our first question for this week is how confident everyone is feeling about the Vikings heading into Week 2 of […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Carson Wentz #11 of the Minnesota Vikings throws a pass during the first quarter against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s time to take a look at the results from our SB Nation Reacts poll for this week, so let’s take a look at how Minnesota Vikings fans are feeling about our favorite football team. Our first question for this week is how confident everyone is feeling about the Vikings heading into Week 2 of the 2026 regular season. You would think that a 17-point victory over a division rival would have folks brimming with confidence heading into the first road game of the season. You would think that. . .and you’d be wrong. Of those who responded to our poll for this week, just 46% feel that the team is moving in the right direction, a drop from 60% going into the season opener against Green Bay. Despite the margin of victory, I suppose that’s understandable given the way that things went. The team was trailing by double digits late in the third quarter, and the Packers pretty well melted down to help the Vikings get the victory in the fashion that they did. Sure, it’s nice to get a huge victory and send a division rival to an 0-1 start to the season, but there are significant reasons for concern as well. Speaking of which, our other question for this week was exactly how concerned everyone is with the Vikings’ offense after their performance in Week 1. Yes, there is some panic to be had among Vikings nation when it comes to that side of the ball. Of our respondents, we had 49% expressing at least a medium level of concern with the offense, so we almost got a majority there. The rest of the distribution is pretty evenly distributed, with 18% with a low level of panic, 17% slamming the panic button pretty significantly, and 16% thinking that everyone should just relax already. There are , as we said, reasons for concern for the Minnesota offense. Jordan Mason is already slated to miss four games after going on injured reserve, Kyler Murray is out after suffering a concussion on Sunday, and in Week 1 only three teams put up fewer yards on offense than the Vikings did. Three of the Vikings’ touchdown drives against the Packers covered less than 30 yards, and overall the level of offensive play we saw from the Vikings isn’t sustainable over the long haul. Hopefully we’ll start seeing some improvements here starting on Sunday in Chicago. Those are your SB Nation Reacts results for this week, ladies and gentlemen. As always, we want to thank everyone who participated in our poll for this week, and be sure to keep your eyes open for the next one! Check out the FanDuel Sportsbook , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation .

The Panthers 3 turnovers surely did not help them out and they lost the time of possession, 34 minutes to 25 minutes. They allowed the Bears to run for 291 yards although 61 came on a long run by Monangia and 29 on a long run by Caleb. Still, stopping the run will be huge. It will be tough on the road but if the Vikings can manage to run the ball a little better even without Mason, then I think that will help tremendously. Containing Caleb will be key as well. It is going to be a great game with a lot of intrigue. You know I am going with the Vikings. Always. There are a few good college games to watch today if you are inclined. At this point, I have to start checking out the QBs a lot closer. Trajectory of 2027 NFL draft QB prospects flips fast https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/49950232/college-football-2027-nfl-draft-qb-prospects-trajectory-flips-fast “This is a really good year to need a quarterback,” another NFL scout said. “Last year was not.” I try NOT to be a homer because I am a huge USC fan. Jayden Maiava looks pretty good. The Trojans have played San Jose State, Fresno, and the Louisiana Rajin’ Canjuns. He has completed 67 out of 83 passes (80.7%) for 896 yards with 10 TDs and 1 INT. Darian Mensah of Miami also is killing it. He has completed 71 out of 79 passes (89.9%) for 873 yards with 11 TDs and no picks.
