Minnesota Vikings News and Links Career-defining season for Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell? https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49964734/nfl-minnesota-vikings-kevin-oconnell-kyler-murray-jj-mccarthy Kevin O’Connell has produced one of the most unique résumés in NFL history. He is the only head coach to deliver multiple seasons of at least 13 victories, as he did for the Minnesota Vikings in 2022 and 2024, without winning a playoff game. … With two significant complications removed — the Vikings fired general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah in January and demoted 2024 first-round pick J.J. McCarthy to third-string QB this summer — will O’Connell take the step this season from a good coach to a great one? … The numbers on O’Connell’s résumé are clear. His .638 winning percentage is the best in team history, and he is tied for the NFL’s fifth-most wins since 2022 despite using nine different quarterbacks. The four coaches ranked ahead of O’Connell benefited from using one primary quarterback over that period. One longtime AFC executive said: “He would have his pick of jobs if they ever fired him.” … ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky said on “NFL Live” this summer that “the quarterback needs to let the star of the offense be Kevin O’Connell,” and further explained his point in a telephone conversation. “There are certain guys that just have a high-end level of play design, playcall and the setup of that playcall,” Orlovsky said. “I played for one of them in Houston, Gary Kubiak. I had never been around a coach that could watch film, know exactly how the team and quarterback could attack the defense, but then in the game within a drive or two, know exactly what wrinkle might be needed and know how to get that wrinkle set up. I think Kevin has that. “Sometimes quarterbacks, because they are highly competitive and incredibly egotistical, think they can make whatever throw. For quarterbacks with this type of playcaller, you’ve just got to get into that rhythm of believing he’s got it.” In an interview this summer, Murray joked that O’Connell can coach “football for dummies” because of how clearly he articulates his concepts and provides answers. That reputation was a factor in the months leading up to the 2024 draft, setting into motion a series of events that could be career defining for O’Connell’s time in Minnesota. … O’Connell pushed hard to trade up from No. 11 to No. 3 to select Maye, but the New England Patriots turned down Adofo-Mensah’s offer. Despite recent speculation that O’Connell opposed drafting McCarthy with a trade up to No. 10, multiple sources said he supported it alongside a development plan that included credible veteran options in 2024 (Darnold) and perhaps beyond. They thought McCarthy, because of his age and perceived room for growth, could eventually be a difference-maker. … Meanwhile, multiple sources said the Vikings were surprised by the degree of McCarthy’s immaturity. O’Connell has hinted publicly at it, noting last season that McCarthy’s feedback during film sessions indicated he was veering wildly off script. O’Connell also did not hide his displeasure with McCarthy’s decision to celebrate a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys 5 yards before he crossed the line of scrimmage. McCarthy’s admission that he did it in part because he had been told not to during practice did not sit well internally. … O’Connell has built and maintained his connection with players based in part on lessons he took from his own disappointing NFL quarterback career. He annually earns top grades in the NFL Players Association workplace survey. Players do not necessarily point to distinctive approaches or special team-building exercises but instead emphasize what feels to them as a deep level of personal connection and substance. “He has a really, really, really unique ability for the entire locker room to buy into the message and the goal and the principles of how we try to do things,” right tackle Brian O’Neill said. “I think he has incredible buy-in and he’s one of those guys that we want to win for him, and not just alongside him. The best way I can say it is it feels like we work together.” This spring, O’Connell began researching potential replacements for McCarthy. The way it happened, Murray told ESPN, immediately earned his respect. “With all the narratives that have been said about me,” said Murray, who was released in March after seven seasons with the Cardinals and one year left on his contract, “KO really dug deep. He talked to people that knew me, really everybody under the sun. … He really studied who I was. And I think he also had his own perspective of me as a player and what I’m capable of. “We live in a social media age where all you see is what you see. He wanted to learn and judge me by himself. I definitely appreciated that.” As he moved through training camp, Murray quickly understood what other players had already concluded about O’Connell’s inherent empathy. “He has a great gauge of guys’ temperament,” Murray said. “And that’s one thing that you can respect, especially as a quarterback. Maybe you didn’t have the best week. As a player, internally, maybe I’m feeling like I didn’t have the best week. I’m frustrated. He’ll pull you aside when he doesn’t have to, but he feels that that guy, whoever it is, might be down.” … Observing O’Connell from afar, Teasley said recently that he believed him to be highly intelligent and to be a “big-picture thinker” as a head coach. After working with him for three months, Teasley said that long-range observation has proved true. “It’s just been really seamless and…

title: Week 2 Roundtable: Minnesota Vikings vs. Chicago Bears
summary: Hello everyone, and welcome to the Week 2 Minnesota Vikings roundtable here at Daily Norseman. The Vikes are coming off an incredible fourth-quarter performance that helped them beat the Green Bay Packers at home in the opener. Can the Vikings beat the Bears and take an early stake in NFC North supremacy? Let’s talk to […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates a fourth quarter touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello everyone, and welcome to the Week 2 Minnesota Vikings roundtable here at Daily Norseman. The Vikes are coming off an incredible fourth-quarter performance that helped them beat the Green Bay Packers at home in the opener. Can the Vikings beat the Bears and take an early stake in NFC North supremacy? Let’s talk to it: Question 1: Buy or sell: the Bears offense is as good as it showed in Week 1? Brandon Warne : No chance. I don’t think we’ll look back at Carolina as a particularly good defense when the dust settles, and while I like the cadre of offensive talent the Bears have under Ben Johnson, even this was a shocking output. This should be a fun chess battle between Johnson and Brian Flores, to be sure. Dave Stefano : Sell. Hard sell. They dropped 59 on Carolina in a game that looked like two high school teams forgot to play defense. That’s not a Week 1 statement — that’s a schedule gift wrapped in orange and blue. Ben Johnson’s scheme is legit and Caleb finally looked comfortable, I’ll give them that. But 59 points against a Panthers defense that couldn’t tackle a parking cone is not the same as lining up against Brian Flores sending the house 78 percent of the time. Ask me again after they see a real front and I’ll decide whether to buy. Right now? That’s a rental. Warren Ludford : The Bears have a good and balanced offense with solid position groups across the board. Having said that, the Panthers defense is poor and allowed the Bears to run up the score with largely routine passing and strong run game aided by more yards from Caleb Williams than normal. Sam Buegler : Sell. I think it will be a great offense, but I don’t think any team could maintain that level for 17 weeks of the season. While they could get close, I don’t think they will beat the average points per game record and will come back to Earth a bit after facing the Panthers. ————— Question 2: Where do you stand on Caleb Williams as an NFL quarterback right now? BW : When he’s accurate and decisive, he’s as good as anyone. When he’s flustered, he looks like a rookie. I guess that doesn’t really make him any different than pretty much any quarterback in the league outside of maybe a few. But I do wonder if he’s the right player to execute Johnson’s offense long-term. Certainly, last week showed he can do it, and he’s possibly the most talented young quarterback in the game. If Johnson keeps tailoring his offense to his quarterback’s strengths and away from his shortcomings, he’s a Pro Bowl-level quarterback. Games against a Flores defense will be the litmus test for whether he’s good or just “good enough.” DS : He’s a very talented young quarterback who just had his best “look at me” game of his career against a defense that invited it. Dual-threat, off-script magic, two rushing scores — all the stuff that made him the first pick. I don’t hate the kid. I just refuse to crown him after one shootout in Charlotte. Year 3 is supposed to be the leap year. Fine. Prove it against Flores, Van Ginkel, and a secondary that just spent four quarters taking the ball away from Jordan Love. Until then, he’s a promising QB who still has to show he can win ugly in a division game, not just pretty against a sieve. WL : Caleb Williams still struggles with accuracy but is getting more comfortable in the Bears scheme. He hasn’t shown much ability to throw with anticipation, as he normally needs to see his receivers open before he throws. But he also has the talent to make sensational off-schedule plays. The downside is these are low-percentage plays. The passes that don’t connect don’t make the highlight reel. But he has a great situation around him offensively and he can improve if he learns to throw with anticipation and becomes a bit less conservative and more accurate with on schedule throws. SB : I think he’s grown into a good QB and is scary, especially once he starts to improvise. This being the second year of the Ben Johnson Experience in Chicago means he is more used to the system, what Johnson is looking for out of him, and has a deeper understanding of the schemes, so I would expect him to have a breakout year. ————— Question 3: Fill in the blank — The Vikings will win if __________ happens? BW : Flores wins the chess match and Wentz does enough good to outweigh the bad. Flores-Johnson should be getting more attention for the heavyweight battle it is, and I still have reservations about Wentz’s accuracy and the decision-making that trickles out from it. Still, there are times when you see flashes of the quarterback who played at an MVP level early in his career in Philadelphia. And part of the inaccuracy could be chalked up to rust; he’s played (and played healthy) so sporadically over the last few seasons that I don’t think it’s shocking that he still might be getting used to the flow of an NFL game again. DS : …Flores keeps sending the blitz and Wentz doesn’t turn it over. That’s it. We don’t need 39 again. We need the defense to keep doing what it did after halftime last week — wreck the pocket, force the throw they want, and let Jefferson and the rest of the skill guys finish drives. If the offense just doesn’t gift Chicago short fields, Soldier Field gets quiet by the fourth quarter. Again. WL : If the Vikings can move the ball effectively on offense and not turn the ball over, the defense and special teams will do their part to secure victory. SB : Wentz can game manage effectively. He needs to not get flustered and pump fake 10 times in a row and instead stay calm, collected, and be able to take what the D gives him. Chicago let Carolina put up 37 points, and Jalen Coker had 138 yards. If Wentz can effectively exploit them similarly, who knows how much Jets and JA could go for. ————— Question 4: Same question, but for the Bears… BW : I think they need to take an early lead. Use the home-field atmosphere to their advantage. Prove that the offense can score against a non-JV-level unit with some regularity. None of this is out of the realm of possible with a Johnson-led offense. DS : …they win if their offensive line actually picks up Flores’ pressure and Caleb doesn’t start hero-balling the second things get tight. Carolina let him scramble for days. Minnesota will not. If Chicago’s line holds up and they can run Swift enough to keep Flores honest, they’ve got a shot. If they try to win a track meet against this defense, they’re going to learn why 59 points in Week 1 doesn’t travel. WL : If the Bears can frustrate the Vikings offense enough and win the turnover battle, their offense should be able to do enough to come out on top. SB : Protect Caleb Williams. The Vikings won 90.6% of their pass-rush attempts last week. If they can keep that up and not give Williams time to cook, the Vikes have a good chance; but if the Chicago line holds up and gives Caleb time to work his magic, we might be in trouble. ————— Question 5: What’s your final score prediction and why? BW : I’m taking the boys in purple, 35-21. I just have a really good feeling about this one. The Vikings are for real. DS : Vikings 27, Bears 23. Ugly, sloppy, divisional football at Soldier Field. Chicago’s going to score — they just put up 59, they’re not going to forget how. But Flores is going to make Caleb uncomfortable, Wentz (or a cleared Murray) is going to manage it just well enough, and somebody in purple is going to make a play late. That’s the script. SKOL. WL : I’m going with the Vikings in an upset, 27-20. SB : 24-20 Vikings. Maybe I am being optimistic and riding off a high of being at the Bank for the opener, but I think that the Vikings strike first, take an early lead, and don’t look back. They bring the Bears back down to Earth and…

title: 5 questions and answers about Patriots vs. Steelers
summary: The New England Patriots return home on Sunday to take on the Pittsburgh Steelers in their home opener. The game is a rematch from last year’s regular season, but there has been substantial change particularly for the Steelers since the two franchise’s last crossed paths in 2025. In order to find out more about the […]
full_text: The New England Patriots return home on Sunday to take on the Pittsburgh Steelers in their home opener. The game is a rematch from last year’s regular season, but there has been substantial change particularly for the Steelers since the two franchise’s last crossed paths in 2025. In order to find out more about the Patriots’ Week 2 opponent, we spoke with Ryland Bickley of Pats Pulpit’s sister site Behind the Steel Curtain , the SB Nation community for all things Steelers. What team-wide effect has Mike McCarthy thus far at head coach? How has his relationship with Aaron Rodgers evolved since the last time they were together? After nearly 20 years under the CEO-like leadership of Mike Tomlin, a lot is different under McCarthy, from big, on-field changes to things as simple as no longer providing an injury report in a postgame opening statement. Obviously, it’s still far too early in the new Mike’s tenure to make sweeping judgements on what has been different, but some things that have been noticeable include assistant coach hires such as Patrick Graham, who has been a breath of fresh air on defense (more on that later), and McCarthy being more hands-on in player development, notably at quarterback. Of course, McCarthy is the Steelers’ offensive play caller, unlike Tomlin, and his offense has looked different from past Steelers teams even if it wasn’t reflected on the scoreboard last week. For starters, there’s already been a bigger emphasis on middle of the field passing, and the run game is more varied than Arthur Smith’s zone-heavy philosophy last year. As for the Rodgers/McCarthy relationship, I can’t speak too much to that as I’m not actually in the Steelers building. But while Rodgers is still no stranger to bizarre headlines, a common theme of his time with the Steelers has been teammates singing the praises of their veteran quarterback. He’s well-liked in that locker room and seems to only be playing because he still enjoys it. On the field, Rodgers did look a lot better than his 2025 self last week, pushing the ball downfield more and being willing to extend plays when needed. The big question this week is if that trend will continue, or if Week 1 was an outlier due to Rodgers facing an undermanned Falcons pass rush. The Steelers’ receivers missed out on some downfield opportunities last week. Are you concerned there may be a long-term issue, or was it just Week 1 rust? Yes and no. Some Week 1 rust was always expected, especially as Rodgers has always been a quarterback who relies heavily on strong chemistry with his pass catchers. That said, despite being built like a jump-ball receiver, DK Metcalf plays more like a pure speed threat. Last week was an especially bad game for him, but his inability to come down with the ball on some tougher grabs wasn’t exactly a surprise, either. Still, he had a brutal, clean drop on an in-breaker that would’ve gone for a chunk play or even a score last week, and I’d expect him to make the catch in the future. Another interesting name is Roman Wilson, a third-round pick in 2024, who looks to be finally making an impact on offense this year as Pittsburgh’s WR3 to open the season. He and Rodgers almost connected on a few plays, but “almost” has been a common theme of Wilson’s NFL career thus far. To sum up my point, the Steelers’ offense showed some big-play potential last week, but it’s still hard to tell if that will actually lead to anything. I’ll add that a pleasant surprise last week was Michael Pittman Jr., who’s hardly a burner at this point in his career, but showed off some good chemistry with Rodgers and a knack for finding soft spots in defenses for big gains. [Editor’s note: Pittman Jr. has been ruled out for the game] Have the Steelers’ offensive line and secondary changes been a net positive or negative? Not to sound like a broken record, but it’s still too early to tell. The offensive line had a rough preseason and some struggles against Atlanta last week, but first-round right tackle Max Iheanachor is still working his way into the lineup and top starters Troy Fautanu (left tackle) and Mason McCormick (left guard) have both switched from playing on the right side last year. That’s led to some understandable growing pains. The group has plenty of talent, especially with Zach Frazier remaining a stalwart at center, but the Patriots should be able to see some success against a weaker right side of the line. The run game was especially rough last week, with the Steelers averaging -1.14 yards before contact per carry — worst in the NFL. As for the secondary, the cornerback room, with Jamel Dean and Asante Samuel Jr. starting on the outside, held up well against the Falcons last week despite the absence of Joey Porter Jr. (also not expected to suit up against New England). Jalen Ramsey has definitely lost a step but remains an above-average defender, playing in the slot in nickel defense and rotating to safety in base. Jaquan Brisker recorded an interception last week at safety and made an impact near the line of scrimmage. The problem, of course, is that the success came against Cooper Rush at quarterback; Drake Maye will be a much bigger issue. While the cornerback room is solid, there’s a real lack of range at safety the Patriots could definitely exploit, and the Steelers are already thin at the position with DeShon Elliott on injured reserve. How has Patrick Graham put his fingerprint on the Steelers’ defense? Do you think they stick to an all-zone approach vs Drake Maye? Graham was running some hilariously complex sim pressures and coverages at times in the preseason, and actually simplified things once Week 1 hit. My take is that the Steelers realized they didn’t have to overcomplicate things to beat Cooper Rush last week, and guessed correctly. Instead, they sat back, let the defensive backs see things unfold in front of them in zone, and took advantage of some miscues on offense. Against the Patriots, I’d expect more varied coverages, but even against Atlanta, a lot of what was classified as zone was match coverages, which have a lot in common with man concepts. Graham does like to play a lot of split-safety coverages, with a heavy dose of cover 4 last week, and I’d expect that to continue in Week 2. Outside of the secondary, Graham is known for helping his inside linebackers succeed in his scheme, and that was on display in Week 1 with Payton Wilson playing one of the best games of his career after a rough 2025. The Steelers have a pair of highly-athletic off-ball linebackers in Wilson and Patrick Queen, and under Graham they’ve been looking a lot more comfortable. Do you anticipate more blitzing from the Steelers against Drake Maye? If not, how do you feel about their ability to affect the quarterback rushing on only four? To parrot my above answer, the Steelers’ defensive game plan was very Falcons-specific last week, and I’d expect Graham to mix things up against New England. Graham himself said more blitzes would be coming when asked about it by the media earlier this week. Still, the Steelers are more capable than most teams at generating pressures with just four rushers. The team’s top three outside linebackers — T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Nick Herbig — are all fantastic players with varying skill sets, and Watt returned to form against the Falcons, winning the AFC Defensive Player of the Week award for Week 1. So far, Graham has done a great job rotating and finding unique usages for all three players, even giving Herbig some inside linebacker snaps at times against Atlanta. Inside, Cam Heyward remains a force in his late 30s with a lethal bull rush. The recently-extended Keeanu Benton has a potent club move and has been growing as a pass rusher, with a career-best 5.5 sacks last season.

(Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots will have a single standard elevation on hand versus the Pittsburgh Steelers. The organization called up punter Mitch Wishnowsky from the practice squad on the eve of Sunday’s meeting at Gillette Stadium. Wishnowsky, 34, gets his second appearance in as many weeks with incumbent punter Bryce Baringer beginning the regular season on injured reserve . The 6-foot-2, 220-pound vested veteran, who signed to the practice squad at its formation , averaged 44.3 yards per punt and 42.0 net yards per punt in his September debut versus the Seattle Seahawks. While also serving as the holder for long snapper Julian Ashby and kicker Andy Borregales on a 50-yard field goal, three of his four punts were downed inside the opposing 20-yard line at Lumen Field. No touchbacks were logged. Selected by the San Francisco 49ers in the fourth round of the 2019 NFL draft at No. 110 overall, Wishnowsky spent six campaigns in the NFC West before making stops with the Washington Commanders and Buffalo Bills. The former Ray Guy Award winner via Australia, Santa Barbara City College and the University of Utah stands 106 games into his career with 352 punts worth 15,997 yards, including a long of 74. The right-footed specialist is scheduled to revert to the practice squad after the home opener. Three standard elevations loom as the league limit before a 53-man roster move would be required from him to take the field. The Patriots ruled out offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover on the final injury report ahead of the Steelers matchup and have since downgraded cornerback Carlton Davis III. Interior offensive lineman Ben Brown and outside linebacker Dre’Mont Jones move forward with questionable game designations. Sunday’s kickoff in Foxborough is set for 1 p.m. ET.

title: 3-Point Stance: The Patriots most crucial to replacing A.J. Brown
summary: Last week, the New England Patriots experienced what life would be like without A.J. Brown this season. It was far from clean. Brown suffered a high-ankle sprain in the third quarter of New England’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks on Sept. 9. Once Brown left the field, the Patriots’ offensive production regressed. Despite holding […]
full_text: Last week, the New England Patriots experienced what life would be like without A.J. Brown this season. It was far from clean. Brown suffered a high-ankle sprain in the third quarter of New England’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks on Sept. 9. Once Brown left the field, the Patriots’ offensive production regressed. Despite holding a 10-0 halftime lead, New England fell after Seattle scored 13 unanswered points . Quarterback Drake Maye struggled to push the ball downfield in the contest. The third-year signal-caller initially threw for 79 yards and one touchdown, completing 11 of his 15 attempts. Then, following Brown’s injury, Maye connected on 12 of his next 18 attempts for 99 yards and gave away three costly fourth-quarter interceptions. Now, with the receiver landing on short-term injured reserve , he’s out for at least four games. And to add salt to the wound, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport expects Brown to miss about six weeks of the season , which would set him up to return on Nov. 1 against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium. How will the team try to fill that void until then? Moving forward, Maye will have to operate without his No. 1 receiver and, outside of Mack Hollins, a trusted wideout like Stefon Diggs or even Kayshon Boutte. A collective effort from the offense as a whole is necessary to compensate for what will be lost. “Any injury that you get at this point in the offseason, you kind of approach it with an all-hands-on-deck approach,” offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said on Saturday ( via WEEI ). “We’ve got a lot of different skill guys who can do a lot of different things. “There isn’t one person on our roster who can replace anybody like A.J. Brown in the middle of a game or for a stretch of the season. We’ll band together, we’ll figure out what we can do well and try to get the guys in positions to play to their strengths.” Still, it all starts with who lines up out wide. Romeo Doubs Free-agent addition Romeo Doubs had a quiet opening to his career in New England during Week 1, unable to record a single catch on his three targets. Lining up on 2nd-and-14 at his own squad’s 22-yard line, Maye rolled out to his right with the game tied at 10 apiece early in the fourth quarter. The quarterback found Doubs wide open for a first down, but the receiver turned his head early and dropped the pass. One play later, Maye threw his second turnover, leading to the Seahawks’ go-ahead field goal. “He dropped a pass. You know what I mean? Everybody drops a pass,” head coach Mike Vrabel said about Doubs on Monday. “Everybody misses a tackle. You talk to him the same way you always talk to him. Figure out a way to make a play to help us win, and he did a lot of great things during camp, just like everybody did. And so, I know he’s excited to get back out there, get to work and to find a way to help us win.” In training camp, Doubs also started slowly and didn’t make much of an impact throughout early practices. It wasn’t until his role changed, working the sideline and receiving more 50/50 balls, that he began stacking positive days. But even though Vrabel seems to remain confident in the 26-year-old, another question arises as to whether he can expand his role. In the absence of Brown, Doubs may be asked to work the middle of the field, short and at the intermediate level, which he did a lot of at the start of camp. Nonetheless, while Doubs has struggled with drops in the past, one performance doesn’t change the fact that he can be a reliable jump-ball target for Maye and excel in the red zone. In his second season with Green Bay in 2022, Doubs caught seven red zone touchdowns, ranking fourth in the NFL. Part of the offense’s success for the time being falls on Doubs finding his footing and potentially adjusting to a larger workload. Kyle Williams The same goes for second-year receiver Kyle Williams, who could help replicate Brown’s ability as a deep-ball threat if his chemistry with Maye improves. Although the pair connected on two deep-shot scores in 2025, their chemistry was largely marked by miscommunication. Moving forward, Williams has an opportunity to establish himself and earn a consistent role on the offense. Despite a quiet season opener, Williams had a standout preseason with that responsibility, catching four passes for 129 yards and three touchdowns. “Sure. I mean, we want to get Kyle involved,” Vrabel said on Monday when asked if Williams’ role may expand . “I’m hopeful that Kyle can find a role for us and find a way to help us, using his speed and catch-and-run opportunities like we saw last year at times, or some shot-type plays. The Seahawks’ defense emphasized downfield coverage last week, focusing on preventing Maye’s deep opportunities, which restricted New England to the short passing game. Maye executed that approach efficiently until he “lost patience” and began forcing unnecessary deep throws. But if the Patriots focus on the short passing game, they still need a downfield threat capable of turning any play into a touchdown. Establishing the short game opens that possibility for a deep play, as Seattle’s defense adjusts to New England’s underneath strategy. TreVeyon Henderson An effective run game also draws defenders closer to the line of scrimmage to allow those attempts, and with TreVeyon Henderson close to returning, he’ll be a key part of that. Henderson sustained an ankle injury during a practice on Aug. 24 and was sidelined through the season opener. Since then, however, Henderson has been a full participant in practices this week and said Thursday that he’s “ready to go.” Similar to Williams, Henderson is another explosive playmaker. During his rookie season in 2025, the running back forced 30 missed tackles and totaled four touchdown runs of over 50 scrimmage yards. It’s unknown whether he’ll be more effective running between the tackles or prove reliable at picking up blitzers and earning more third-down snaps. Regardless, Henderson always has a chance to take any touch to the house.

title: College Players to Watch: Week 2
summary: The Saints showed on Sunday that there are still some areas they need to improve. Here are some college prospects to keep an eye on going into the Week 2 matchup who could be making major strides early this football season. DB is a position where you can never have enough talent. KJ Bolden is […]
full_text: BATON ROUGE, LOUISIANA - SEPTEMBER 5: Ty Benefield #2 of the LSU Tigers celebrates after a play against the Clemson Tigers at Tiger Stadium on September 5, 2026 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Photo by Ella Hall/University Images via Getty Images} The Saints showed on Sunday that there are still some areas they need to improve. Here are some college prospects to keep an eye on going into the Week 2 matchup who could be making major strides early this football season. DB is a position where you can never have enough talent. KJ Bolden is a name that should always stay on the radar. This nickel/safety is very versatile and is a key contributor in a Kirby Smart defense, so he should transition into the NFL very well. Bolden and the Bulldogs will be playing against Arkansas at 11 a.m. on Saturday. Tae Johnson is another safety with size and range. Johnson plays for Notre Dame and will be facing off against Michigan State on Saturday night at 6:30 p.m. Ty Benefield is a fast-rising safety at LSU. He is very experienced, but he is also a first-off-the-bus type of defender. Not only does he look the part, but he can play multiple positions across the secondary. He can play down in the box, deep off the ball or even in the slot. Benefield will be in Oxford taking on the Rebels on Saturday at 6:30 p.m. Linebacker is another position group on the defense that needs to be watched as well. Sammy Brown is a name that should be remembered. Brown is a physically gifted linebacker who can cover every single blade of grass and does not have to come off the field on third downs. Brown will be playing against North Carolina on Saturday at 11 a.m. Chris Cole is another name to watch for Georgia. Who wouldn’t want a linebacker coming out of Georgia? Cole has length at the position and can affect the passer in pass-rushing situations, but he’s not just a pass rusher. He can still play traditional linebacker as well. Georgia is playing Arkansas, so you can get a two-for-one by watching this game. We talked about cornerback last week and went over Leonard Moore. Here are two other names to watch out for. Ellis Robinson IV, yes, another Georgia Bulldog. Robinson is a long, rangy, athletic corner. He can hold his own in press-man situations and cover zones very well. Again, he plays in a Kirby Smart defense. Kelley Jones at Mississippi State is probably the best player on the defense, if not the team. His frame and athleticism started to showcase themselves near the end of last season, and if he follows that up with another good year, expect him to shoot up NFL Draft boards. Jones will have a good matchup on Saturday against South Carolina with Nyck Harbor and LaNorris Sellers at 3:15 p.m. The offensive line did not look that good in the game against Detroit, so here are two names to watch for this week. Trevor Goosby and Jordan Seaton are both star tackles with elite size and athleticism who are also great pass protectors. Goosby plays for Texas, and the Longhorns will be playing against UTSA on Saturday at 7 p.m. Seaton plays for LSU and will be with Benefield in Oxford facing off against the Rebels at 6:30 p.m. on Saturday. What are some other names you’re keeping your eyes on this weekend? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

title: Patrick Ricard makes Cam Skattebo feel ‘safe,’ more NY Giants notes
summary: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo likes to run into — and over — things. That’s fun and stuff, but moms worry about their boys. Which is why Skattebo’s mom loves full Patrick Ricard, Skattebo’s personal bodyguard on many of his runs. “I feel safe,” Skattebo said of running behind 300-pound ’Pancake Pat’. “When […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo tkes a handoff from Jaxson Dart. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo likes to run into — and over — things. That’s fun and stuff, but moms worry about their boys. Which is why Skattebo’s mom loves full Patrick Ricard, Skattebo’s personal bodyguard on many of his runs. “I feel safe,” Skattebo said of running behind 300-pound ’Pancake Pat’. “When he hits the first linebacker and I don’t have to take them both on, it’s really nice. “My mom – when we first signed Pat, my mom didn’t really know who he was at first. And then I kind of showed her some videos and kind of taught her what he was going to be doing. And she goes, ‘I want to meet that guy.’ So, my mom says it’s safer, and me, 300 pounds in front of me as a lead blocker on top of the o-line is awesome. It feels awesome.” Tyrone Tracy, kickoff returner When Deonte Banks was in and out of the Giants’ lineup against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 1, the Giants turned to Tyrone Tracy to join Braxton Berrios as one of the two kickoff returners. It is a job Tracy has done before, with eight kickoff returns over the past two seasons for an average 24.1 yards per return. Perhaps the only surprising part of Tracy getting that call is that he had fumbled the ball away on his second — and last — carry of the game against Dallas. He also had a fumble in a preseason game. Banks is questionable to play vs. the Rams with a calf injury. Even if he does play, the Giants might not want to risk using him on kickoff returns. So, we could see Tracy regularly in that role. “Just gives us the running back, the vision. A guy, again, that can run returns downhill. They’re downhill plays. And a guy that can bounce off tackles,” said special teams coordinator Chris Horton. “We just want guys that have a lot of skill, guys that can make plays on their own, and guys that can make people miss in the hole. Because a lot of times it’s going to be one guy that you might have to make miss.” But, the fumbles? “Not concerned at all,” Horton said. “Just things that we talk about. Just from a fundamentals standpoint, you’re going through traffic, let’s make sure we protect the ball.” "It's a question we're asking ourselves, in all honesty. I think it comes back to what he's capable of handling." John Harbaugh was asked how close Malik Nabers is to being able to handle a full workload: pic.twitter.com/2k7s6YDz8w — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 18, 2026 Is Malik ready for more? Malik Nabers led the Giants with nine targets in Week 1, his first game back from last season’s torn ACL. Nabers, though, played only 36 of 68 snaps, 52%. Is Nabers ready for more? “It’s a question we’re asking ourselves, in all honesty,” said head coach John Harbaugh. “I think it comes back to what he’s capable of handling. He had a good workload today again, so as he’s ramping up his volume in practice, which would be bringing him closer to that kind of mindset in the games, we’ll see as we get through the games. He looks strong. He does.” Nikko’s adventures New Giants cornerback Nikko Reed was signed off the Los Angeles Chargers’ practice squad on Thursday. Reed hopped on a flight from Los Angeles to New Jersey, practiced with the Giants on Friday and Saturday, then got on a flight back to LA on Saturday afternoon for the team’s trip to LA to face the Rams. I wonder if Reed is still on West Coast time. Harbaugh seemed happy to acquire Reed. “It’s good to be aggressive, especially at that position,” Harbaugh said. “There’s still guys on the practice squad who won’t last on the practice squad probably too much longer, so it was a good get for us.” Numbers to know The Giants’ offensive linemen gave up 10 pressures across 192 combined pass-blocking snaps, third-lowest in the NFL in Week 1. The Giants surrendered the third-lowest quarterback pressure precentage, 5.2. The Giants have a 10-game streak of gaining at least 100 yards rushing, longest in the NFL. The Giants’ 81.82% third-down conversion rate against the Dallas Cowboys led the NFL and was the team’s best since 1991. The Giants were fifth in the NFL in total yards allowed (244) and rushing yards allowed (69) in Week 1.

title: NY Giants expect returning Aaron Donald ‘to play like Aaron Donald’
summary: Aaron Donald is expected to make his return to action on Monday for the Los Angeles Rams after a two-year retirement. So, what are the New York Giants expecting from the nine-time All-Pro and 10-time Pro Bowler? They are expecting Donald, 35, to be the great player he was during his initial 10 years in […]
full_text: Aaron Donald | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Aaron Donald is expected to make his return to action on Monday for the Los Angeles Rams after a two-year retirement. So, what are the New York Giants expecting from the nine-time All-Pro and 10-time Pro Bowler? They are expecting Donald, 35, to be the great player he was during his initial 10 years in the NFL. “Expect him to play like Aaron Donald, which is a game-wrecking type player inside,” Giants head coach John Harbaugh said. “Penetrating, active movement player who can wreck the game, really any particular play in a lot of different ways, run and pass. So, we’re expecting him to play. We’re planning for him to be out there.” Donald said this week that he is “feeling good”, and the “the plan” is for him to play. Donald tried to downplay his potential impact, or the idea that he would get extra attention from Giants blockers. “You think they’re going to double/triple team me [after] not playing for two years? They ain’t worried about me, man,” Donald said. “They don’t have to be worried about me. They don’t have to worry about me at all. No man, they don’t have to worry about me. “Whatever happens, I’m just going to go out there and play my game and just try to do what I can do. I don’t know what they’re going to do out there. I don’t know what I’m going to get. All I can know is I got a game plan. I’m going to go out there, execute it, and just try to play ball. That’s it.” The Giants will, of course, give etxra attention to one of the greatest defensive linemen of his generation. Giants left guard Jon Runyan has played against Donald before. Runyan, rookie right guard Francis Mauigoa, and center John Michael Schmitz will have primary responsibility for containing Donald whenever he is on the field Monday night. Runyan understands what Donald, even a rusty Donald, can do. “He’s a really unique player for the defensive tackle position. He’s not the biggest guy, he’s listed as 6 foot, I don’t really know if he’s even 6 foot, 285, super strong, super athletic, super fast,” Runyan said. “He gets the ability to kind of play how he wants, jump around blocks, and he’s good at that. “He’s out there to make plays. Great pass rusher, obviously. Very physical, strong, good with his hands, and he’s just on a different level when it comes to understanding, leverage, using his strengths, like his speed and his hands. He diagnoses everything really fast, and that’s why he’s been doing it at a high level for so long, and probably one of the best to do it of all time.” Donald will likely play a limited number of snaps. “I’ll probably be a lot more fresh. I’ll probably be fresh. It’s a long year, long season,” Donald said. “We have a lot of good football players out here. My game plan is, however it’s going to be, I’m going out go out there and play hard. And when I need a break, tap out, let the next guy go out there and eat, and I’ll be right back. I think we have a good game plan to get myself going and get this team going. Whatever that role is, I’m ready for it. I’m excited about it and I’m just going to do it.” Quarterback Jaxson Dart has watched enough football, and looked at enough film, to understand the kind of player Donald has been. “For the longest time that I can remember, he’s one of the most dominant players that I’ve watched,” Dart said. “So, getting the chance to go out there and compete against him, it’s going to be really cool just to be on the same field as him. He’s a great player, and I’ve heard that he’s kept himself in really good shape. So, it’s going to be a great competition. “The real impact on the game from just a game plan standpoint, there’s countless clips of putting three offensive linemen on him and still being able to make a play. So, he’s an unbelievable player and has had an unbelievable career.” Running back Cam Skattebo understands there will will likely come a time during the game where he meets Donald in the hole on a run play. “I’m excited to play against him. He’s one of the best to ever do it. It’s going to be fun. It’s going to be a good challenge for the guys up front. It’s going to be a good challenge,” Skattebo said. “If I have to meet him in the hole on third and one, then so be it. I’ve got to get one yard. But he’s a good player. He’s one of the best to ever do it. So, all respect to him.”

full_text: Welcome to the New York Giants betting angle, Week 2 edition! Each week, I’m giving you my three favorite wagers for that week’s New York Giants game. My one rule: I won’t ever give you wagers that are less than -120. No gimmes! The Giants travel to Los Angeles this week for a Monday Night Football matchup with the Rams. For both teams, it’s a second straight showing in prime time. Things went about as well as they could have for the Giants at home against Dallas in Week 1, while the Rams got smoked in Australia by the 49ers. Much has been made of Los Angeles’s travel decisions around that game. They’ve got an 11 day recovery window from that experience before hosting Big Blue on Monday. The Rams, who came into the season as one of the Super Bowl favorites, are favored by 7.5 points, with a game total of 47.5. I went 2-1 last week, thanks to the UNDER sneaking in by half a point. A good start to the season, and I’ll take it, Brandon Aubrey! Let’s get to this week’s picks. All lines and odds are from Fanduel and are as of Friday, Sept. 18. Giants + 7.5 (-118) . I don’t want to overreact to Week 1, but this feels like a lot of points for the Rams to lay. L.A. lost Myles Garrett in Week 1 and while they’ll get Aaron Donald into the lineup for this one, I think Jaxson Dart and the Giants should be able to score enough points to keep Big Blue in the game. I like getting the TD plus the hook, and even if New York is trailing by more than a score, the backdoor cover is in play. I think New York is a live dog with a legit chance to pull off the upset. Give me the points. Malik Nabers OVER 5.5 receptions (-114). Nabers was uncertain to play right up until a few hours before gametime last week, and in the end he was only on the field for 52% of the Giants’ offensive snaps. He still hauled in six catches on nine targets. He’s always going to command a massive target share when he’s out there, and I expect his snap count to tick up each week as he acclimates. New York ran the ball a lot last week, as they were playing with a lead for the entire second half. That probably won’t be the case this week. Six catches feels like a fairly easy bar to clear. Davante Adams longest reception UNDER 19.5 yards (-114). Adams is not only no longer a deep threat, he’s no longer a target hog. His receptions over/under for this game is just 3.5. That line, coupled with the low volume he got last year and in Week 1, suggests limited opportunities and that makes me feel better about him not catching anything 20 yards or longer. Those are the picks for Week 2. Good luck with your wagers! And if you play fantasy football, be sure to check out my Week 2 fantasy preview, with start/sit advice and more, right here.

title: College football Week 3: Draft prospects to watch for the NY Giants
summary: ollege football Week 3 Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 3 of the 2026 College Football Season. There are certainly some interesting games on today’s slate, but there’s one that will dominate the conversation: Ole Miss vs. LSU. Before we get to that game, however, we have a couple […]
full_text: Rutgers wide receiver KJ Duff makes a catch against Penn State | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect ollege football Week 3 Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 3 of the 2026 College Football Season. There are certainly some interesting games on today’s slate, but there’s one that will dominate the conversation: Ole Miss vs. LSU. Before we get to that game, however, we have a couple others to highlight. As usual, we’re looking at college football from an NFL Draft and NY Giants perspective. So while there will be plenty of intriguing prospects on the field, I want to concentrate on prospects play at (what could be) positions of perceived need for the Giants. Today that means Safety and pass catcher. Everyone is, of course, encouraged to use this as an open thread to discuss all of college games, but we’ll only be highlighting three players specifically. Arkansas vs. (2) Georgia ABC – noon Highlight Player – KJ Bolden (S, Georgia) It will be interesting to see how the Giants’ secondary evolves over the course of the 2026 season. However it plays out, Joe Schoen and John Harbaugh will have some tough decisions to make. Cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome II are on one-year deals, and it could be expensive to bring both back if they both prove to be good starting corners over the course of the season. Likewise, Nickel Ar’Darius Washington is on a one-year deal as well, while Dru Phillips, Tyler Nubin, and Jevon Holland are all free agents after the 2027 season. Georgia’s KJ Bolden is almost custom-built to be a modern NFL nickel defender. He’s listed as a safety, but he is legitimately excellent in coverage as well as in run defense. He’s a bit lean at 6-foot-1, 185 pounds, but plays with a high football IQ, fast processing, and violence at the point of attack. Rutgers vs. (12) USC CBS – 3:30 p.m. Highlight player: KJ Duff (WR, Rutgers) Rutgers fans and alumni might want to avert their eyes from this game. But for the rest of us, I need to call attention to a potential Giant right in their own back yard. WR KJ Duff is flying under the radar right now at the national level (that tends to happen when your school isn’t playing well). However, he has the traits to work his way into the conversation with Texas’ Cam Coleman and Indiana’s Charlie Becker in the next tier of wide receiver prospects after Jeremiah Smith. Duff is listed at 6-foot-6, 225 pounds and comes in at 22nd on the 2026 edition of Bruce Feldman’s “Freaks List” for his strength and agility. Duff is surprisingly agile on tape and reportedly put up a 4.16-second short shuttle time over the summer. For reference, the average short shuttle for a wide receiver is 4.23 seconds — and at 6-foot, 200 pounds. He had an impressive 60-catch, 1,084-yard, 7 TD season as a sophomore in 2025, and could be a real sleeper if the Giants want to add yet more size to their offense in 2027. (8) Ole Miss vs. (7) LSU ABC – 7:30 p.m. Highlight player – Trey’Dez Green (TE, LSU) This game is high drama… Or maybe melodrama that’s more suitable for a daytime soap opera. The story of the game is going to be the return of Lane Kiffin to Ole Miss following his messy exit and the chaos surrounding his willingness to accept former NFL players who fell through the cracks in the NCAA’s eligibility rules. On the field, the story will be quarterbacks Trinidad Chambliss and Sam Leavitt. These are two talented, athletic, and competitive passers who each have the potential of being first round picks come April. Chambliss is a far more advanced passer than he was given credit and is definitely the better player right now. However, Leavitt has the kind of mobility and arm talent that will draw comparisons to Caleb Williams, albeit in a much more volatile package right now. For our purposes, however, I want to concentrate on LSU tight end Trey’Dez Green. Green is the best tight end in the class and be the next “Brock Bowers” or “Tyler Warren” when he enters the NFL. He’s a former basketball player with elite athletic traits at 6-foot 6 3/8 inches tall, 240 pounds, with great long speed as well as agility. Green has the route running skills to separate and is already the most prolific tight end in LSU history, owning both their single-season and career touchdown records — in just 25 games with 9 starts. Green is still developing as a blocker and is much more of a “move” blocker than a traditional Y tight end. However, given how often the Giants use pulling blockers now, that’s not necessarily a bad thing. The potential of pairing Green with Isaiah Likely and Theo Johnson is definitely tantalizing.
author: Chris Pflum

title: New York Giants mailbag: First impressions, retired numbers, penalty reviews
summary: Bob Donnelly asks: It’s great to see the Harbaugh era start with a W and there’s certainly a lot to get excited about. I’m sure there are some in the glass half empty crowd that will say that the W is nice and John is 1 and 0 in one score games, but there remains […]
full_text: Bob Donnelly asks: It’s great to see the Harbaugh era start with a W and there’s certainly a lot to get excited about. I’m sure there are some in the glass half empty crowd that will say that the W is nice and John is 1 and 0 in one score games, but there remains some of the latent issues that often derailed this team last year with ball security (4 fumbles , 2 turnover-worth plays) and penalties (#1 penalty yards) leading the list. As you reflect on the first game performance under Harbaugh what areas concern you most? Ed says: Bob, absolutely nothing has changed from my preseason evaluation of the Giants. The biggest areas of concern entering the season were cornerback play and defensive line depth. Nothing about Sunday changed that. Tae Banks was OK. I thought he got pushed off on the touchdown he surrendered. I didn’t think Greg Newsome was that good against the Cowboys, but he was a lot better than Paulson Adebo. Colton Hood still isn’t ready for full-time duty. DJ Reader and Shelby Harris were fine. When they were replaced by Darius Alexander and C.J. Okoye, Dallas had more success running the ball. If they can find a run-stuffing veteran defensive tackle who can help them get through this season that would be great. Adam Jacobs asks: I have an offbeat question about the taunting penalty by Javonte Williams. Every penalty that occurs in the field of play is marked at the spot of the foul unless it occurs behind the line of scrimmage. Except the Williams penalty. Why was this enforced after the play was finished, and not from the spot of the foul? I am not sure I have ever seen this before. Do you have any idea how this works? Ed says: Adam, taunting is treated as a dead-ball foul. Thus, the result of the play stands. The penalty is assessed after the play. Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, I know teams can request a review of penalties after the game. Not that it will change any results, can you explain how this process works? Ed says: The NFL audits every snap during the days after games, looking at calls and non-calls. That is both to assess the performance of the offcials, and to determine discipline when it comes to handing out fines. NFL teams can send a maximum of 10 plays to the league office each for review, clarification, explanation. Sometimes, the league will admit that a mistake was made. That, though, will not affect an outcome or result in a do-over. James Pauloski asks: For me, the most amazing statistic from the Cowboys game was that Dallas only had two possessions in the second half. Yes, they scored two touchdowns, but that was it. That seems almost impossible. Did the Giants tie (or set) a record for allowing only two possessions in one half? Ed says: James, I have been unable to find anything to answer that directly. What I can say is that each team had only seven possessions on Sunday, making 14 total (yes, I can do math!). That is an incredibly low total. There was a 2023 game between the Denver Broncos were there were only 12 possessions, six for each team. It speaks to efficiency by both offenses as there were five drives in the game that took more than six minutes, two of those by the Giants lasting more than eight minutes. Todd Kuehn asks: Ed, I really like looking at box scores when the game is over because the information and numbers in them are all objective instead of subjective except for two of them. Maybe I’m wrong about that but when you look at the QBR and the RTG for quarterbacks from the Dallas game it seems to me maybe they are subjective. Dart got a really good RTG 134.2 and Prescott only had 84.8. But when you look at the QBR Dart received 81.5 and Prescott had an 89. How can that be? There is no doubt in almost everyone’s mind that Dart outplayed Prescott. Ed says: Todd, there is no perfect quarterback measuring stick. PFF uses a different methodology than QBR, passer rating, etc. As Tony DelGenio pointed out this week , Pro Football and Sports Network’s ‘Impact Score’ had Dart as the second-highest rated quarterback this week with Prescott 14th. It all depends what they are grading and with they give importance to. Bottom line is that no matter how Dart was graded by any rating system, it was clear that he played very well and did the things needed for the Giants to win a football game against a good team. Martin Hand asks: Hi Ed, I just saw an article about Gronkowski and that his number had not been retired yet… It made me think about our situation with Malik and Abdul… Don’t you think it is a bit self-absorbed for an retired individual to think that the number is his and does not belong to the franchise… Players last a few years, whereas the Giants will last forever… I don’t have my heels dug in over this one, but couldn’t help to think about it and wanted to ask you what you thought. Ed says: Martin, I can’t say I have ever heard that opinion before. Players don’t decide to retire their numbers. Franchises do that in honor of those players. So, yes, the number belongs to the franchise and that is what the franchise has chosen to do with it. To be honest, I vehemently disagree with the whole idea of “unretiring” numbers. I think sometimes well-meaning franchises retire too many numbers. Here is the list of Giants’ retired numbers . I think the Giants allowed Malik Nabers to wear the previously retired No. 1 jersey opened a Pandora’s Box that led to the Abdul Carter mess, and that it won’t be the last time there is a situation like that. Numbers, though, get retired because of a player’s accomplishments. That means something to that player, and to the player’s family. Why should a kid fresh out of college who has done nothing get the number of an all-time franchise great? Because his “brand” revolves around that number? Please. Jeffrey Jacobs asks: Do you see any scenario where the Giants mange to pry Joey Porter Jr. away from the Steelers, and if so what do you think it would take? Ed says: Jeffrey, of course there is a scenario where the Giants try to pry Porter Jr. away from the Steelers. I think it is highly unlikely, but if the Giants believe the player is worth the draft capital they would have to surrender and the big price tag they would have to pay him they would try to make it happen. Spotrac recently posted what their model believes Porter’s price tag would be: Trading CB Joey Porter Jr. New Team Acquires 2026: $3.5M 2027: UFA #Steelers Dead Cap 2026: $1.4M The 26-year-old projects toward a 4-year, $110M extension according to our model. — Spotrac (@spotrac) September 18, 2026 Four years, $110 million would make Porter the seventh-highest paid cornerback in the NFL in terms of average annual value. Is he really worth that kind of money? Also, the Giants are extremely reluctant to give out contracts of that length. Andrew Thomas and Brian Burns, arguably the two best players on the team not currently on four-year rookie contracts, are the only veteran players with deals of longer than three years. Are the Giants really going to go there for Porter? Remember, not too far down the road they will have to negotiate long-term deals with Jaxson Dart, Malik Nabers, and Abdul Carter. As for trade cost in terms of draft capital, I can’t imagine the Steelers being able to drive a hard bargain for Porter if they choose to move him. I am not offering more than an early-Day 3 pick considering the contract I would have to give him. Marcus Mbow bonus I was asked many times during the offseason if I knew whether or not second-year offensive tackle Marcus Mbow has put on weight during the offseason. Until Thursday, I couldn’t answer the question because I had not spoken to him at all. I got a chance to speak with him for a minute in the locker room this week. For all of you obsessed by Mbow’s weight, he put on 15 pounds this offseason and is now around the 320-pound mark. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

title: Jets vs Packers Pre-Game Ball
summary: We’re going to try something new here. Plenty of people hand out game balls after the game. That’s easy. Watch the game, see who does well, give them the game ball. Let’s do something a little more difficult. Let’s hand out a pre-game ball. Before we watch the game, let’s settle on one player we […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Kenyon Sadiq #16 of the New York Jets scores a rushing touchdown against James Williams Sr. #52 of the Tennessee Titans Tennessee Titans during the first quarter of the game at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re going to try something new here. Plenty of people hand out game balls after the game. That’s easy. Watch the game, see who does well, give them the game ball. Let’s do something a little more difficult. Let’s hand out a pre-game ball. Before we watch the game, let’s settle on one player we think might be a decisive advantage for the Jets in the upcoming game. Occasionally we might hand out a pre-blame ball. If we think the Jets are going to get slaughtered, we’ll try to identify a prime culprit. One caveat: the quarterback is off limits. Nothing personal against quarterbacks, but they are obviously the most important players on the field. We could give out a pre-game or pre-blame ball to the quarterback virtually every week, but that would be boring, so we’re not going to do it. We’ll try to identify somebody besides the quarterback for the glory or the ignominy. This approach comes with the obvious drawback that predictions are difficult, especially about the future. We’ll probably get most of these wildly wrong. No matter. We’ll have some laughs along the way. So without further ado, let’s get to it. The inaugural Jets pre-game ball for the Jets game against the Green Bay Packers goes to (drum roll please) – Kenyon Sadiq. This game might be a bit early for a Sadiq breakout. He missed virtually the entire offseason for the Jets and is still getting integrated into the offense. No matter. Go big or go home, right? Since I’m already home, I’m going big. The Green Bay Packers have struggled recently defending against tight ends. Last week T.J. Hockenson and Josh Oliver combined for 6 receptions for 56 yards and a touchdown. Last year, in 18 games including the playoffs, the Packers gave up 105 receptions for 902 yards and six touchdowns to tight ends. Against teams that featured better, more athletic tight ends, in nine games the Packers gave up a combined 57 receptions for 552 yards and four touchdowns. Those came against a combination of Sam LaPorta, David Njoku, Harold Fannin, Jake Ferguson, Tre McBride, Dallas Goedert, Mark Andrews, Isaiah Likely and Colston Loveland. Kenyon Sadiq has obviously not yet earned a place among the NFL’s best tight ends yet, but he is more athletic than any of those guys, and has the potential to swiftly rise up the ranks. Why not start the rising right now? The Jets are down to just four wide receivers today. Two of the four, Isaiah Williams and Arian Smith, have yet to make an impact as NFL receivers. The Jets will likely respond to the lack of established targets at wide receiver with a bunch of heavy, multiple tight end sets. They showed last week they wanted to get Sadiq involved in a variety of ways early, despite his lack of practice reps. Why not make this Sadiq’s coming out party? This is probably way too early for the rookie, but what the heck? Let’s have some fun. Kenyon Sadiq, come on down! Let’s see you light up the Packers on a dreary, rainy Sunday afternoon in East Rutherford. You get our first ever pre-game ball. Try not to drop it. What about you? Who would you give the pre-game ball to? Let us know in the comments.

title: Jets vs Packers Game Day Forecast
summary: The New York Jets are at home in East Rutherford, New Jersey for the 2026 home opener today. They will be taking on the Green Bay Packers. The game is scheduled to start shortly after 1:00 pm EDT. The game will be played in cool and rainy weather. Cloudy skies will prevail for the entirety […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 28: New York Jets fans react during the first half of a preseason game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on August 28, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets are at home in East Rutherford, New Jersey for the 2026 home opener today. They will be taking on the Green Bay Packers. The game is scheduled to start shortly after 1:00 pm EDT. The game will be played in cool and rainy weather. Cloudy skies will prevail for the entirety of the game. Winds will be moderate and variable at around 5 to 10 mph with a few higher gusts out of the south southeast to start the game, shifting to the south in the second half. Temperatures will be in the mid 60s to start the game, increasing to the upper 60s as the game progresses. Relative humidity will be very high, in the lower to mid 90% range throughout the game. There will be an 85% chance of rainfall to start the game, decreasing to 70% by game’s end. The rain will fall at a fairly steady, moderate rate. The cool and rainy conditions will make sharp cuts on the field more difficult for the players. The ball will also be slippery, potentially contributing to some dropped passes and perhaps some turnovers. In general, rainy conditions favor the running game, particularly a power running game, and negatively impact the passing game. With the rain not expected to be particularly heavy, however, the weather’s impact on the game should be fairly minimal for the players. For the fans the cool and wet conditions aren’t ideal. Umbrellas or some waterproof attire should go a long way towards making things more comfortable in MetLife Stadium. Enjoy the game everyone.

title: Three things I’m looking at in the Jets vs. Packers game
summary: Heading into this Week 2 showdown, the vibes are sky-high, and the fanbase has plenty of hope. For me, who prefers to live in the comfort of truth and reality rather than emotion and pandemonium, it’s legitimately tough to properly contextualize this Jets season so far. Luckily for us, my colleague addressed that very issue […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 09: Zack Kuntz #88 of the New York Jets is tackled by Corey Ballentine #35 of the Green Bay Packers during the second quarter during the NFL Preseason 2025 game between New York Jets and Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on August 09, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into this Week 2 showdown, the vibes are sky-high, and the fanbase has plenty of hope. For me, who prefers to live in the comfort of truth and reality rather than emotion and pandemonium, it’s legitimately tough to properly contextualize this Jets season so far. Luckily for us, my colleague addressed that very issue for all of us, and I’m at peace with my hopefulness for this Sunday! As we discussed before Week 1 , this isn’t meant to be a prediction. It’s not necessarily “three keys” to the game. It’s an approach to looking at the game outside the mainstream narrative, and I guarantee you’ll learn at least one stat you’ve never seen before. The 0-1 Green Bay Packers will be traveling to MetLife Stadium for the home opener against the 1-0 New York Jets. This is super exciting; not only are the Jets undefeated, but the way they beat down the Titans last week gives all of us tangible hope that the dog days may finally be over. A quick glance at accuweather.com shows lots of rain and wind on the horizon for the game, which will surely play a role in this game. Can the Green Bay Packers, one of the league’s most prestigious organizations led by one of the game’s most respected coaches, bounce back after an embarrassing second-half collapse last week? Are the Jets, the perennial “butt of the joke” in professional sports, finally ready to become relevant? Was the shellacking of the Titans a foreshadowing, or a random outlier? Let’s take a look: What’s Love Got to Do With It? Everyone is quick to point out that Jordan Love was sacked four times in Week 1 and use that as the basis for the “Swiss cheese offensive line” argument, but no one adds the caveat that his 42 passing attempts were the second-most in the NFL last week. Love was sacked on less than 10% of his dropbacks, which is much more respectable than, say, Malik Willis, who was also sacked four times but only had 27 dropbacks (15.6% sack percentage, 2nd most in the league). Still, Matt LaFleur’s signal caller can still succumb to pressure and make poor decisions. Only one team in the NFL blitzed more than 50% of the time last week: Brian Flores’s Minnesota Vikings, who blitzed the Packers on 33(!) of those 42 dropbacks (71.7% blitz percentage). We saw both the pros and cons of such a blitz-heavy attack: Love had two turnovers and was sacked several times, but he also had a few explosive plays that gave him the second-most yards of any QB and the league’s longest play so far (81 yards). I’d imagine and hope Aaron Glenn shows more restraint than Flores (30.8% blitz percentage) and is more strategic about deploying blitzes. If Week 1 is any indication, we should all feel great about the chances of this happening. The Jets were a top-3 team in the NFL in YAC (yards after catch) allowed and missed tackles, meaning that regardless of whether they blitzed, a Jet was still in the area to make a sound tackle and prevent extra yardage. With a rushing attack that totaled only 66 yards on 21 carries, the Packers are probably expecting to throw a lot of passes again, even with the rain. Step 1 for the Jets is to continue their run-stuffing ways (they allowed only 68 yards last week), and from there it will be a chess match between LaFleur and Glenn on when to dial up pressure for Love without leaving his secondary vulnerable. Luckily for us, this is a coaching matchup that used to happen multiple times per year when Glenn was the DC in Detroit. Glenn and his new personnel should have an easier time preparing for generally the same Packers running the same offense than the Packers would have preparing for an entirely new group in NY executing his system from Detroit. Is the Safety on? One of the few pieces of bad news from last Sunday was the loss of All-Pro Minkah Fitzpatrick, who fell to a groin injury early in the game. As a result, Andre Cisco and Dane Belton played more snaps, and both did well with the additional game plan. Now, with a full week of game planning against them and much more offensive talent than the Titans, will the Packers flip the script on this unit? Christian Watson has been one of the league’s most prolific deep-threat WRs from day one, and he currently has the longest touchdown of the season with 81 yards. Next Gen Stats lists his top speed during that run at 21.09 MPH, the third-fastest speed of a ball carrier this season so far. His combination of size and speed is perfect for his role, and he continues to punish teams over the top of the defense. Matthew Golden seems to be finding his footing in the offense, and the Packers also acquired TE Jonnu Smith in the offseason. Smith is another dynamic blend of size and speed who scored a touchdown against the Jets for the Steelers in that Week 1 contest last year. The year before that, he was a Dolphin, and he scored in each game he played against the Jets, including a game-winner in OT. All of these players are certainly more dangerous than Gunnar Helm, Wan’Dale Robinson, and a Carnell Tate playing in his first-ever game. Watson, Golden, and Smith each had at least one 40+ yard reception last week, and I outlined Jonnu’s recent history against the Jets. He’s not even TE1; Tucker Kraft (21.5 yards per reception) will be out there too. I also want to stress that this is a matter of air yards – Jordan Love had the second-most air yards per attempt in Week 1 despite having the fourth-fewest seconds to throw (2.56). The Vikings tied the Jets for the league’s second-fewest missed tackles last week, so this wasn’t a matter of guys running loose after a short screen. This was Matt LaFleur getting guys open downfield and Love having the arm to drive it downfield consistently against a talented (albeit outnumbered) Vikings secondary. Neither Cisco nor Belton were particularly spectacular in pass coverage last year, and we can be certain they will be tested. The rain should help minimize these opportunities, since throwing slick balls 30+ yards in the pouring rain isn’t ideal, but I still expect them to be aggressive. Cisco had seven picks 2022-2023, and Belton has had at least one interception in each of his four previous NFL seasons, so maybe the actual rain can create an opportunity to end the metaphorical drought (of interceptions). D’Angelo Ponds is set to make his debut this week, and I’m sure the Jets will welcome as much assistance in the secondary as possible. It will take a whole-team effort, but I’m mostly talking about the safeties, since they’re the last line of defense against an offense that specializes in deep balls downfield. Let’s Kick It I was pleasantly surprised to see Jason Sanders start the season 2/2 with extra points and 3/4 with field goals, including two makes from 50+. We were all done with him, and it looked like the Jets’ coaches were too, until he was named the starter a few days before the season opener. I took that as a roll of the dice and hoped that the team would go for it on 4th and keep Sanders’s kicks inside the 40. Yes, his one miss was absolutely atrocious, but 11 points and 83% total accuracy is a solid day at the office! He alone outscored the Titans. As we all know, rainy games mean a lot of rushing attempts, but they usually mean a lot of kicks as well. Will Sanders get to keep his job through this storm? The last rainy game at MetLife I can clearly remember was the 2024 Week 4 showdown with the Broncos, which ended in heartbreaking fashion for Jets fans. If you ask me, that game completely turned the season upside down. Rodgers, coming off two straight wins and four touchdowns, couldn’t drive the team downfield for a touchdown in the rain.…
