title: NFL Week 2 betting guide: Top plays for Sunday afternoon's games
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 2 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 1.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week  | Solak's plays  | Walder's props 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 Cincinnati Bengals at Houston Texans (-2.5, 46.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Reliant Stadium, Houston

 

 This line has fluctuated but at -2.5, I am all-in. Would I feel the same at -3? I wouldn't love it, but I'd be willing to bet Houston at home in a bounce-back game after the Week 1 loss to Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills . Let's get into what to look for on both sides of the ball, and we'll finish with some props bets to play.

 

 When Houston has the ball: Houston spent the offseason working on its run game, trading for David Montgomery and adding to the offensive front. And we saw a dedicated effort to run the football in Week 1, as Montgomery had 20 carries, with Woody Marks chipping in with nine. Now, was it super efficient? No. Montgomery averaged just 3.0 YPC, and the Texans registered a run block win rate of 74% (17th in the league). But it's clear that Houston wants the run game to be a foundational element of its offense. This can boost the passing opportunities for quarterback C.J. Stroud , who will see a Bengals defense featuring a rebuilt front anchored by defensive tackle  Dexter Lawrence II and an underrated secondary that can mix both zone and man looks. I would look for play-action concepts (which mirror the run game) to attack the Bengals' two-deep zone shells while also scheming up some shot plays. With Nico Collins out, the scheme won't change in Houston.  Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte can work the interior in-breakers while Jaylin Noel operates out of the slot. I truly think Houston looks to control the tempo on offense in this one, but let's keep an eye on third downs because the Texans need to beat man coverage from the Bengals there.

 When Cincinnati has the ball: I want to see this matchup against the Texans' defense. Though the Bengals looked flat in a Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers ( Joe Burrow finished with 254 yards passing, and Ja'Marr Chase had two receptions for 12 yards), they create conflict because of scheme and talent. The Texans have been a zone-heavy defense under DeMeco Ryans, but they will mix in man coverage (based on game situations), which creates must-see TV when corners Derek Stingley Jr . and Kamari Lassiter match against Chase and Tee Higgins . Tight end Mike Gesicki (78 yards receiving in Week 1) could find room to operate against Houston's split-safety and single-high zone schemes to attack the voids there. But, my main question is will the Bengals' offensive line keep the pocket firm for Burrow and generate movement up front in the run game? The Bengals held a pass block win rate of 53.8% in Week 1 against the Bucs (13th in the league), while Chase Brown averaged only 3.5 YPC. It's a different matchup this week against Houston edge rushers Will Anderson Jr . and Danielle Hunter . Burrow will need to hit some explosive play throws to win this one.

 Leans: Texans -2.5 (-118), Texans moneyline (-142), Over 46.5 (-105)

 Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

 Ja'Marr Chase receptions OVER 6.5 (-109) 

 I expect a dedicated effort to get Chase the ball after he caught only two of four targets in the Week 1 win over the Bucs -- screens, unders and quicks that cater to Chase's explosive catch-and-run ability. Look for Chase to be involved early in this game plan.

 Mike Gesicki anytime TD (+280) 

 Gesicki caught a Week 1 touchdown on a schemed throw to beat man coverage. Plus, the Bengals can set up Gesicki on zone beaters in the high red zone (seams, corners) to counter the Houston defensive tendencies.

 Chase Brown receiving yards OVER 20.5 (-113) 

 Brown caught five of six targets for 22 yards last week versus Tampa, and the screen game/swing routes could be an early answer to counter the Texans' pass rush.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Green Bay Packers -3.5 (-112) at New York Jets 

 I'm grabbing a quick buy-low spot on the Packers, who were much better Sunday than the box score would indicate. The Minnesota Vikings scored 14 late points on defensive takeaways deep in Green Bay territory in their 39-22 victory. But the Packers had a better success rate (38.8%) than the Vikings (34.5%) and struggled only in situational spots. They were 3-for-12 on third down. On four red zone trips, they scored only one touchdown and one field goal. Those are the little execution problems that hurt a box score.

 

 Going from facing a Brian Flores-coached Vikings defense to the Jets should make things far easier. Matt LaFleur has experience facing Aaron Glenn from when Glenn was the defensive coordinator of the Detroit Lions and generally has found success (46% offensive success rate, 0.04 EPA per play, 2.2 points per drive).

 I thought about taking the Packers' team total, currently priced at 23.5 and juiced -135 to the over. I think the Jets' offense will be a functional group this season, but they need to run the ball and play clock control to win games against superior opponents -- and that might limit the Packers' total drives. As such, I'll go instead for the full-game spread at -3.5. I would play this no further than -120.

 Tennessee Titans team total UNDER 15.5 (-105) 

 The Titans' offensive operation was the worst I saw in Week 1: play designs that were dead in the water, offensive linemen uncertain of their assignments, easy drops and bad routes from receivers and poor accuracy and timing from Cam Ward at quarterback. It's tough to find anything to hang their hat on from a 23-10 loss to the Jets.

 

 It's worth remarking that Brian Daboll's offenses have been poor in Week 1 -- six, six and and zero points in the three seasons previous -- and then stronger in Week 2. But against this Philadelphia Eagles  defense, it's tough to have much faith. Philadelphia's defensive front looked as deep and disruptive as ever against an average Washington Commanders front, and the Titans are comfortably one of the eight worst lines in football. Though defensive back Cooper DeJean was banged up in the Week 1 game and sat out practice Wednesday, the Eagles' outside corner duo of Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen still poses a huge problem for the Titans' ability to create explosive plays through the air.

 The talent difference here feels simply insurmountable. The Titans will need defensive takeaways or big special teams outputs to get into scoring range. I don't see them getting enough. I would play this up to -115.

 New England Patriots -5.5 (-105) vs. Pittsburgh Steelers 

 The past four defenses the Patriots have faced are as follows: Seattle Seahawks (Week 1), Seahawks (Super Bowl), Denver Broncos (AFC Championship Game), Houston Texans (AFC divisional round). Even their wild-card opponent had a near-elite defense ( Los Angeles Chargers ). We are finally at a point at which we can buy low on the Patriots against an imperfect defense.

 The  Pittsburgh Steelers ' defense was hardly tested in Week 1 against the Cooper Rush -led Atlanta Falcons . Drake Maye and the Patriots' offense --…

title: Who are the top 10 players without a Super Bowl ring?
summary: Introducing our Super Bowl Top 10s. First, we rank the best players who never won a championship, beginning with Dan Marino.
full_text:
Every NFL player has the same goal: win a Super Bowl ring.

 But football is the ultimate team sport, and with the exception of maybe someone such as  Tom Brady , it's hard for one player to will his team over the championship finish line. In the NFL today, active players such as Baltimore Ravens ' Calais Campbell (19th season) and New Orleans Saints ' Cameron Jordan (16th season) are still chasing a Super Bowl ring. Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (ninth season) has taken his team to the AFC Championship Game twice in eight tries and ran into Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs dynasty both times.

 

 How hard is it to win a Super Bowl? We ranked 10 of the best retired players who played at least half their careers in the Super Bowl era but never won a ring. Some of them made multiple appearances in the big game and came up just short, while others never made it beyond the conference championship. The methodology, which utilized Pro Football reference approximate values, included ESPN analyzing the statistics and intangibles of players in the Super Bowl era who didn't win a ring and put together a list ranking the best of the best.

 Here are 10 of the best players in NFL history who finished their careers without a Super Bowl win. Let's start with a Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback who spent his career with the Miami Dolphins .

 COUNTDOWN TO SUPER BOWL LXI: ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February. We are counting down to the big game with a Super Bowl Top 10 series -- featuring rankings on everything from best catches and performances to biggest upsets -- that will run every other Sunday leading up to Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, 2027. 

 

 No. 1: Dan Marino, quarterback 
 Teams played for: Miami Dolphins (1983-99)

 What you might have forgotten: Marino's 1984 season was the gold standard for quarterbacks for years to come. Quarterbacks chased after Marino's single-season record of 5,084 passing yards for more than 20 years before Tom Brady and Drew Brees passed it in 2011. That 1984 season, Marino's second and his first full season as a starter, is still considered one of the best seasons by a quarterback. He led the NFL in passing attempts (564), completions (362), passing touchdowns (48), passing yards (5,084) and rating (108.9), among other records. 

 Number of Super Bowls Marino appeared in: 1 (Super Bowl XIX)

 Just how close did he come to winning a ring? Marino came into Super Bowl XIX with a 14-2 record as a starter that season and an MVP award. Unfortunately, he had to face the San Francisco 49ers ' Joe Montana in his prime. Both quarterbacks passed for more than 300 yards for the first time in the game's history, but Montana's 339 passing yards and 59 rushing yards were too much to overcome in a 38-16 win by the Niners.

 The Dolphins made it to two more AFC Championship Games, and Marino didn't play well in either of them, finishing with a 54.9 passer rating in a 31-14 loss to the New England Patriots in the 1985 AFC Championship Game and a 56.5 passer rating in a 29-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills in the 1993 AFC Championship Game.

 Marino retired with an 8-10 record in the playoffs after 17 seasons with the Dolphins.

 

 Marino said it: "That was the burning desire. That is what I played for," Marino said on the day he retired in March 2000. "That has been a dream of mine my whole career. I wanted to know -- as a player -- how it feels to win a Super Bowl."

 Why Marino is ranked No. 1: Though Marino's postseason play could be cause for debate, at his peak, he put up numbers that would still be respectable among quarterbacks today in a league that favors offenses. His 1984 season is among the greatest for a quarterback, but it ended without a ring due to the performance of another future HOF quarterback.

 

 No. 2: Barry Sanders, running back 
 Teams played for: Detroit Lions (1989-98)

 What you might have forgotten: The 5-foot-8 running back was picked third by the Lions in the 1989 draft, selected by a team whose last playoff win was 34 years before he got there. Sanders never had a Pro Bowl quarterback in his pro career, but he ran behind All-Pro left tackle Lomas Brown.

 Sanders, whose elusive running style gave defenses fits, abruptly retired on the eve of the 1999 season after making 10 All-Pro teams and winning two NFL Offensive Player of the Year honors and a shared MVP award with Brett Favre in 1997. Sanders retired with 15,269 rushing yards, the second most in NFL history at the time and still fourth all time. His 18,190 yards from scrimmage ranks seventh.

 Number of Super Bowls appeared in: 0

 

 Just how close did he come to winning a ring? Sanders' third season was his best chance for a Super Bowl appearance after the Lions made it to the NFC Championship Game, but the Lions were soundly defeated 41-10 by Washington. Sanders rushed only twice in the second half and finished with 11 carries for 44 yards. The Lions' 38-6 win against the Dallas Cowboys in the 1991 NFC divisional round was their last playoff win until the 2023 season.

 Sanders said it: "I had already achieved a level of success that gave me much satisfaction and pride. I didn't need to pass Walter [Payton and the career rushing record] to prove that to myself," Sanders wrote in his book : "Barry Sanders: Now You See Him ... His Story in His Own Words." 

 Why Sanders is ranked No. 2: Sanders left the game with the impression that he still had a lot more to give. His career is full of what-ifs -- what if he had played longer, or for a more successful team? While 30 is often considered an age in which running backs decline, Sanders had 1,780 all-purpose yards that final season. He never reached the physical point of no return -- he simply chose to walk away . 

 

 No. 3: Anthony Munoz, left tackle 
 Teams played for: Cincinnati Bengals (1980-92); Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1993 preseason)

 What you might have forgotten: When Munoz went into the Hall of Fame in 1998, he was described as "one of the most dominant offensive tackles in NFL history." Munoz was a big reason the Bengals had a run of sustained success in the 1980s. With Munoz paving the way for quarterback Ken Anderson, the Bengals' offense transformed from a bottom-two unit in his first season to a top-three group in Year 2.

 Number of Super Bowls appeared in: 2 (Super Bowl XVI, XXIII)

 Just how close did he come to winning a ring? The Bengals were one of many teams that lost to Montana and his Super Bowl successes with the Niners. Cincinnati turned the ball over four times in a 26-21 loss to San Francisco in Super Bowl XVI. The Bengals faced Montana again in Super Bowl XXIII, and he took the Niners on a 92-yard scoring drive late in the fourth quarter to win 20-16.

 

 Munoz said it: Last year on the "NFL Players Second Act Podcast," Munoz said all he wanted was a chance despite his injury history. The Bengals gave it to him, and three days into camp, the third pick in the 1980 draft realized he had greater ambition. "I told myself, I don't only want to compete, I want to be the best. I want to be a Pro Bowler every year," he recalled . 

 Why Munoz is ranked No. 3: How much impact can a left tackle have? The Bengals had seven top-10 offenses and four playoff appearances when he was there, and their 1990 win in the AFC wild-card round was their last playoff victory until the 2021 season. But Munoz, who earned 11 consecutive All-Pro and Pro Bowl nods, wasn't just a great tackle. He caught four touchdown passes and had a long career despite multiple knee surgeries before he turned pro. Munoz was named to the NFL's 100th Anniversary team in 2019.

 

 No. 4: Dick Butkus, linebacker 
 Teams played for: Chicago Bears (1965-73)

 What you might have forgotten: Mean, tough and nasty are just some of the adjectives to describe the linebacker. He had the shortest career of anyone on this list, playing nine years and 119 games. Butkus retired in 1973 at 31…

title: Ranking all 32 backup NFL quarterbacks for the 2026 season
summary: We stacked the best No. 2 quarterbacks across the league, including Mac Jones and even a few backups who have already been forced to play in 2026.
full_text:
The very first game of the 2026 NFL season provided an important reminder about backup quarterbacks: They don't really impact a team's chance to win ... until they do. And then they suddenly  really do.

 Sam Darnold getting injured early in the Seahawks' season opener against the Patriots forced Drew Lock into action. When Kyler Murray suffered a  concussion   against the Packers  later in Week 1, the Vikings turned to Carson Wentz . Both teams went on to win with their respective second-stringers. In both instances, the defense likely carried the winners more than anything else, but had the offense collapsed with the backup QB, there would have been no hope. The Falcons, who started QB3  Cooper Rush   against the Steelers last Sunday with both  Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr . out , can attest to that.

 With backups already playing a big role early in the season, I've decided to rank each team's No. 2 QB. It's a tricky exercise because we're operating on severely limited information in many cases. Some of these players haven't played in a meaningful pro game in years. Some of the younger backups don't have much regular-season experience at all -- if any. So the margin for error is large. But that shouldn't prevent us from doing these rankings -- after all, teams must make choices about their backups with similarly scarce information.

 So, here is my ranking of every team's No. 2 quarterback. I included Wentz and Lock, but I used Penix as the Falcons' backup for the purpose of this exercise (though I also noted where Rush would land if he were the true No. 2).

 

 

 1. Fernando Mendoza , Las Vegas Raiders 
 This was the easiest decision. Sure, we haven't seen Mendoza take a snap in a regular-season game, but being the No. 1 draft pick is worth enough to easily put him at the top. He has the highest upside of any QB on this list. And if I had to ask any backup to win a few games right now , I would take Mendoza. Drake Maye was in this spot in this exercise two years ago ; it's fair to say that the Raiders would be thrilled if Mendoza took Maye's track. Funny enough, the player who was No. 1 in last year's version of these rankings is Kirk Cousins , the man in front of Mendoza on the Las Vegas depth chart.

 
 

 

 2. Marcus Mariota , Washington Commanders 
 If a team needs to get through a couple games while their starter is out, there is probably no more reliable veteran backup than Mariota. He started eight games (and played in 11) for the Commanders last season when Jayden Daniels was hurt . Mariota recorded a 50.4 QBR and has posted a 57.4 QBR since 2022. That's about as good as it gets for a non-starter, and I thought the Commanders got a steal when they re-signed Mariota to a one-year, $7 million contract this offseason. He's still only 32, too.

 
 

 3. Mac Jones , San Francisco 49ers 
 Currently enrolled in the Kyle Shanahan School of Quarterback Development, of which Darnold is a notable alum, Jones raised his stock last season while filling in for Brock Purdy for eight games. He recorded a 62.7 QBR and a plus-3% completion percentage over expected (per NFL Next Gen Stats). Those are incredibly strong numbers and, taken on their own, would indicate a surefire starter. But he is not one currently because of his previous track record -- Jones recorded a 37.6 QBR from 2022-24 for the Patriots and Jaguars after a strong rookie year with New England in 2021 -- and the assumption that a large portion of his improvement can be directly attributed to Shanahan.

 
 

 4. Spencer Rattler , New Orleans Saints 
 Even though the Saints were 1-7 in games he started last season, Rattler showed significant growth from his 2024 rookie campaign. He sported a 50.8 QBR (up from 37.1 in 2024), a plus-3% completion percentage over expected (up from minus-10%, per Next Gen Stats) and a 9% off-target rate (down from 20%). Considering his youth, Rattler still has upside. I wouldn't be surprised if he gets a shot to compete to be a starter -- even if it's not in New Orleans -- in the next year or two.

 
 

 5. Michael Penix Jr ., Atlanta Falcons 
 Penix could be Atlanta's starter over Tua Tagovailoa after both return from injuries , but he would be very high if he ended up as Atlanta's No. 2. He has had his ups and downs in the NFL but has started only 12 games and is a mere two years removed from being a top-10 draft pick. So, there's potential. And there are things to like about his numbers -- a 55.7 career QBR along with a low 4.1% sack rate. The accuracy hasn't been there (21% off-target rate and a minus-4% completion percentage over expected), but his youth gives him time to improve if he can recover from a  torn ACL suffered last November, his third dating to college.

 
 

 6. Jameis Winston , New York Giants 
 Winston is well into the second phase of his career as a high-end backup. His results have been solid in aggregate, though his play style ensures a roller-coaster ride. Over the past four seasons, Winston has recorded a very high 3.9% turnover rate but still managed a 49.7 QBR in that span. This is because he's willing to push the ball downfield. Winston's 9.6 air yards per attempt since 2022 is higher than any qualifying quarterback registered last season.

 
 

 

 7. Jalon Daniels , Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Is this a reach? Maybe. But undrafted rookies face serious headwinds making rosters, much less being in potentially important roles . So, the fact that Daniels beat out Jake Browning (my No. 2 backup last year ) is a major point in his favor. It's a far stronger signal than a middle-round pick landing a backup job partially due to the draft capital used on him.

 The preseason tape is incredibly enticing, too, with Daniels spinning out of pressures like Russell Wilson , making throws on the run and ripping the ball downfield between defenders. His value is team-dependent. He is a less helpful backup for a Super Bowl contender because he's riskier than many of the players below. But he also has a lot more upside.

 
 

 8. Mitchell Trubisky , Tennessee Titans 
 He had a very limited run of playing behind Josh Allen in Buffalo the past two seasons, but Trubisky had seven starts the two seasons before. Over the past four seasons, he recorded a 54.7 QBR and a plus-4% completion percentage over expected. Those numbers, plus Cam Ward 's struggles in his first season-plus, would actually  raise the Titans' Football Power Index ranking if the team announced Trubisky as the starter for an upcoming game.

 
 

 9. Tyrod Taylor , Green Bay Packers 
 We must bake in some aging downside for the 37-year-old Taylor, but if a team has to get away with playing a backup for a few games, it could do much worse. Over the past four seasons, Taylor's 49.9 QBR and plus-2% completion percentage over expected are pretty good. And his willingness to throw the ball downfield (13% of his attempts go 20-plus air yards, a high rate) and scramble frequently gives him some variance that is useful for backups.

 
 

 10. Tyler Huntley , Baltimore Ravens 
 I've always liked Huntley, but his stock dropped precipitously in 2024 when he bounced among several teams. But he returned to the Ravens in 2025 and saw action in a few games, including two starts. He played very well in that limited span, recording an 81.1 QBR -- good enough to earn a  new contract  from Baltimore with $3.5 million fully guaranteed.

 
 

 11. Mason Rudolph , Pittsburgh Steelers 
 Rudolph originally won the Steelers' backup QB job seven years ago . Since then, he left Pittsburgh before returning last season. And even though the Steelers have changed coaches, Rudolph is their backup yet again. His 53.6 QBR over the past four seasons ranks fourth among players on this list. He throws short -- 6.5 air yards per attempt and past the sticks only 36% of the time -- but the aggregate results are solid.

title: How to bet Colts-Chiefs on 'SNF': Analysis, tips and favorite plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet Colts-Chiefs on "Sunday Night Football."
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have a problem that goes beyond losing 41-23 to the Baltimore Ravens in Week 1. They couldn't get the Ravens off the field. Indianapolis allowed 506 yards and 7.9 yards per play, including 202 rushing yards at 5.5 per carry. Now they go from dealing with Derrick Henry and Lamar Jackson to a Kansas City Chiefs offense that might have finally found the rushing attack it has been missing. Kenneth Walker III ran for 173 yards in his Chiefs debut, helping K.C. pile up 220 rushing yards against Denver.

 

 If Indianapolis has to commit extra bodies to stopping him, that's when Patrick Mahomes gets favorable looks off play-action against a secondary still incorporating new players.

 For the Colts, the counter is Jonathan Taylor , who ran for 98 yards and two touchdowns against Baltimore. Indianapolis needs him to keep this game on schedule. The worst-case scenario is falling behind early and putting the game entirely on Daniel Jones , who managed just 166 passing yards in Week 1.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 I am more interested in the total than laying 6.5 with Kansas City. Both offenses have clear ways to attack the opposing defense. Kansas City can lean on its upgraded rushing attack against a Colts front that entered the season with major questions, which should also create favorable opportunities for Mahomes.

 

 Indianapolis can contribute, too. Taylor gives the Colts a way to stay efficient on early downs, while Kansas City's rebuilt secondary is still the vulnerable part of an otherwise strong defense.

 That creates opportunities for Alec Pierce vertically, Josh Downs underneath and Tyler Warren over the middle. OC Shane Steichen also matters here. His offenses have consistently been aggressive early in games and efficient in the red zone, so Indianapolis doesn't necessarily need Jones to produce a huge passing day to score.

 If the Colts can get into the low-to-mid 20s, Kansas City has enough matchup advantages offensively to push this game over the total.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Patrick Mahomes passing yards OVER 220.5 (-113) 

 Eric Moody: Mahomes finished with just 184 passing yards in week 1 against the Broncos, with only 37 of those going to wide receivers. I expect Kansas City to get its aerial attack going against the Colts. Lamar Jackson threw for 324 yards against Indianapolis in Week 1, and Mahomes threw for 352 against the Colts last season. Mahomes averages 248.4 passing yards per game since 2024, well above this week's line.

 

 Kenneth Walker III rushing yards OVER 80.5 (-111) 

 Maldonado: The stronger look is sticking with K.C.'s newfound strength. Week 1 showed a potentially meaningful schematic change that fits both Walker's skill set and this matchup. I'm less interested in the 173 rushing yards last week than I am in how he got there.

 Walker had 23 carries, forced 14 missed tackles and produced 179 total yards after contact, according to PFF tracking. Not dependent on a single run concept, with 10 zone carries and 13 gap carries, the Chiefs showed a commitment to Walker and a diversified run scheme that created plenty beyond what was blocked.

 Now Walker faces a Colts defense that showed serious problems at the point of attack, including poor Week 1 run defense grades from DTs DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart . The potential game script supports another heavy workload.

 

 Tyler Warren receiving yards UNDER 46.5 (-114) 

 Ben Solak: Warren has not cleared this number since Week 10 of last season, when Daniel Jones had yet to fracture his fibula (let alone tear his right Achilles). Even in an ideal game script last week against Baltimore in which the Colts were trailing all game and needed to throw their way back into contention, Warren saw only five targets. He also doesn't see downfield targets the way he did to start his career (his 4.4 air yards per target in Week 1 was well below his 2025 season average of 5.56). The Chiefs have a strong defense overall, and that running game should limit the total number of Colts possessions.

title: What to expect from Patriots QB Drake Maye vs. the Steelers
summary: New England wants Maye to be patient but aggressive. Can he have success against the daunting Pittsburgh defense?
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Maye's response: Among quarterback  Drake Maye 's endearing personality traits is a willingness to peel back the curtain and share core parts of his mindset. One example is how he said the season-opening loss to the Seahawks on Sept. 9 -- in which he threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter -- was tough.

 Because the Patriots played on a Wednesday, arrived home early Thursday morning, and players weren't in meetings again until Sunday, it extended Maye's moving-on process.

 "You got a lot of time to think about it," he said.

 

 Maye usually gives himself 24 hours to move on from a performance that didn't meet his personal standard. He said he thinks about it Sunday night, watches the game over Monday, and then you "kind of get rid of it."

 It sets up the top storyline for the Patriots entering Sunday's home opener against the Steelers ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ): How does Maye respond?

 By last Monday, he had taken a page from Bill Belichick and told sports radio WEEI, "We're on to Pittsburgh." Teammates took note of Maye's move in that direction.

 "I've seen a guy that came back to work. I haven't seen him like he's walking around with his head down or anything like that," said veteran safety  Kevin Byard , who is one of six captains along with the 24-year-old Maye.

 In doing so, Maye highlighted the "heightened consequences" of when he makes the wrong split-second decisions, such as on each of his three interceptions when he forced plays down the field. Coach Mike Vrabel noted that Maye "can't get bored doing the right thing."

 Therein lies the balance Maye aims to strike against a Steelers team that won its opener over the Falcons 20-13 on the strength of its defense, led by T.J. Watt , Cameron Heyward , Jalen Ramsey & Co. He must stay disciplined and patient to take what's there against a Steelers unit that has forced multiple turnovers in nine games since the start of last season (third most in the NFL) but not hesitate to attack down the field when the opportunity presents itself.

 Those opportunities down the field should be there based on recent history.

 Since the start of the 2025 season, opponents have completed 51% of throws 20-plus yards downfield against the Steelers (ranks 31st in NFL), according to ESPN Research. Meanwhile, Maye has completed 50% of passes 20-plus yards down the field since the start of last season, which ranks third among 32 qualified quarterbacks. But Maye was 0-for-3 on those throws in the opener against the Seahawks.

 Offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels highlighted how Maye is in a different situation compared to last year because opponents have had a full year to study an entire season of his play in the current offensive system.

 He stressed patience and repetition when it comes to Maye making better decisions as the defense changes its look after the snap, which is something the Seahawks did successfully. He added the Patriots want Maye to be "aggressive and smart, and always at the same time."

 "I have not experienced anything with him that he has not learned from when it hasn't gone our way," McDaniels said. "I know this is an area where we can make progress. I know he does, too. I'm excited to see it happen and get another opportunity this week."

 

 2. Hollins/Maye combo: Vrabel made the point late last week that one of the most important things for a quarterback/receiver duo is to "think alike," and Maye and veteran Mack Hollins often do. Perhaps contributing to that: They sit next to each other in the front row of the team meeting room.

 "At the last facility it was like that, so we just kind of sat like that [in the new one]," Hollins said.

 Hollins is most likely to start in A.J. Brown 's place until Brown returns from his right high ankle sprain.

 "I would imagine he'd be a big part of our success going forward," Vrabel said.

 3. Raridon review: Three topics with tight end Eli Raridon , the third-round pick who played 38 offensive snaps and four special teams snaps in the opener, and scored the season's first touchdown on a 2-yard reception:

 
 College vs. the NFL: "Coach Vrabel always reiterated to me the speed of the NFL game is completely different and takes some getting used to. Camp, joint practices and preseason games helped me integrate to that a lot, but at first when I got here, I was like, 'Everything is happening a lot faster.' That's partly because you're learning a new offense. And the level of competition. These guys you're going against are great players. In college, at Notre Dame, we played Miami and [Texas] A&M -- two really good teams. Then you play Syracuse, where we beat them 70-7 and I was out at halftime. It's not like that in the NFL." 
 Speed of the opener vs. Seattle: "That first drive was kind of a whirlwind. The first snap, you're adjusting to 'this is how it is.' It took a few plays to get used to it." 
 Empathic TD spike: "Honestly, I don't really remember too much of it. I just remember kind of standing for a moment, soaking it all in, and I was like, 'I have to do something.'" 
 
 4. Byard's bag: Veteran safety  Kevin Byard  says he has kept the football from every interception he has had in the NFL -- 36 in the regular season and one in the playoffs. They are in a large trash bag in his attic, to be displayed in some form upon his retirement.  Patrick Mahomes , Lamar Jackson , Dak Prescott and Josh Allen are among the top QBs he has picked.

 "Definitely looking to get my first interception against Aaron Rodgers ," Byard said. "But really, I just want to win."

 5. OL dinners return: Patriots offensive linemen started a tradition last season in which they had a weekly dinner each Thursday, which has returned this year. Mastro's Steakhouse & Ocean Club and The Capital Grille were the first two restaurants. Veteran Greg Van Roten , 36, picked up the tab as the oldest player in the room.

 Walter Rouse , whom the Patriots acquired from the Vikings in a trade in late August, said the Vikings did something similar each Thursday although not at such upscale steakhouses.

 6. Gilmore on Gonzo: Former Patriots cornerback Stephon Gilmore signed a ceremonial one-day contract to retire as a member of the organization Friday, saying it was important to him because New England was where he had his greatest success. Gilmore attended the team's practice Friday, celebrated his 36th birthday Saturday and stayed in town for Sunday's home opener with his family.

 The 2019 NFL Defensive Player of the Year, Gilmore is sometimes cited as having a similar approach to current Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez . The two connected in recent days.

 "He's super kind of quiet, kind of like I was, but handles his business on the field," Gilmore said. "He's a great talent -- fast. And has great size for a corner. I think he's going to have a great career. I told him, 'No matter what, stay hungry. No matter what you did last year, you have to prove yourself each and every year. That's what the great players do.'"

 

 7. AVT assessment: The opener was starting left guard  Alijah Vera-Tucker 's first game since the 2024 regular-season finale with the Jets, as he missed all of last season after tearing his left triceps. A lot of hard work went into getting back on the field. Vera-Tucker finished the opener with a 68% run block win rate (179th out of 225) and a 86.2% pass block win rate (tied 90th out of 163), according to ESPN Research.

 "First game back, it just felt really good to be out there, especially with a team and staff like this," he said. "Definitely always things to work on -- more than I would have liked to have happen last week. I have to get better in practice and translate it to the games."

 8. Hot Germany ticket: The Patriots' game against the Lions, to be played Week 10 in Munich, ranks fifth in highest average sold ticket price at $644, according to Vivid…

title: Jets WR Garrett Wilson sheds slot, makes move back to outside
summary: Wilson hopes to avoid hits and be able to deliver more explosive plays on the perimeter.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- A look at what's happening around the New York Jets :

 1. Role shift: Garrett Wilson is back in his comfort zone, back on the perimeter and back in the position where he expects his big-play production to increase.

 So long, slot.

 Wilson lined up as a slot receiver on only four of 46 offensive plays (9%) in last week's opener, a significant drop from his first four seasons (29%).

 This represents a philosophical shift, which began last season, when he mentioned to coach Aaron Glenn that he'd like to be used more often on the outside. Wilson huddled with new offensive coordinator Frank Reich, who was on board.

 "I think it just makes sense," Wilson told ESPN. "I ended up catching a lot of passes these past three, four years at 4 yards, 5 yards, and my back's to the defense and I get smacked after. I can do that, and it's cool, but it's just back to my roots for me.

 "It's more like playing true receiver, that one-on-one game with the corner. You end up catching more passes down the field, and you're just more away from all the -- I'm not a huge guy. Those guys in the interior, the defense, are big guys. It just gives me more space to operate, which I like a lot. I think that's where I'm my best."

 It's not like Wilson struggled in his previous role. In fact, he became only the 10th player in NFL history to record 1,000 receiving yards in each of his first three seasons, and he probably would've done it four straight if it weren't for a knee injury that cost him 10 games last year. The numbers are more impressive when considering he has played with nine different quarterbacks.

 But now that he's playing almost exclusively on the outside, in an offense that he enjoys, with a quarterback not afraid to throw deep ... well, he's a very happy camper. He doesn't have to worry about a slot-corner blitz. He doesn't have to block in traffic. He can just do his thing -- "my natural game," he said.

 "It's a long season, and we're going to end up doing a lot, but being back outside is definitely refreshing," Wilson said. "It makes that film when I go home a lot more simple. Did you beat that DB? Did you finish the play? How open were you? I'm just able to watch my route, which is kind of cool."

 He caught six passes for 79 yards in the opener, including five for 73 on the outside.

 

 2. Statement game: It's the home opener Sunday. The opponent is the Green Bay Packers , a perennial playoff team. It's a chance for the Jets to be 2-0 for the first time since 2015, the league's second-longest active drought. (The Cleveland Browns haven't been 2-0 since 1993.)

 It's a chance for Glenn & Co. to change the narrative.

 "I think each week, we're trying to make a statement; it doesn't matter who it is," Glenn said. "I think we all know our history, and we're trying to change that history."

 That history includes only 11 2-0 starts in the 66 years of the franchise.

 The Jets were impressive against the Titans, but the Packers represent a step up in weight class. As Wilson said, "For us to have a good opponent like this, coming back home, it'll be big for us. We want to earn our respect in this league, and you do that by playing good football every week."

 3. Start of a home run? The Jets have been trying to establish a home-field advantage for what seems like forever. You know what would help? A victory in the first one.

 They've won only three of their past 10 home openers, tied with the Browns, Titans and New York Giants for the fewest from 2016 to 2025, per ESPN Research.

 4. Q's rating soars: What a month for Qwan'tez Stiggers .

 On Aug. 11, he passed out during a joint practice with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and was taken by ambulance to a local hospital. On Sept. 13, he made a few key plays on special teams, including a fumble recovery and downing a punt at the Titans' 2-yard line.

 Afterward, he got a loud shoutout from Demario Davis , who, in a locker room speech to the team, said Stiggers' toughness embodies the mindset of the team.

 In training camp, Stiggers was diagnosed with heat-related vasovagal syncope, a condition that causes sudden fainting because of a temporary drop in blood pressure and heart rate. Before the Titans game, which was played in 90 degree heat, he made sure to load up on fluids and carbs.

 "I got kids, I got a wife, I got little brothers and sisters and stuff, so it kind of causes you to just take a step back and look at life," he said, recalling last month's scare. "I especially look how far I came and just evaluate that and evaluate my future. I'm pretty sure I know I got more years in front of me than behind me.

 "Thank God I'm here."

 Stiggers was a feel-good story in the 2024 draft, getting selected despite having no college experience. He played in the CFL for a season before becoming a fifth-round pick by the Jets.

 5. No vacation: Glenn dialed back training camp compared with the previous year, but he has ratcheted up the regular-season practices. Davis said these are "some of the hardest practices" he has experienced in 15 seasons.

 He wasn't complaining; he said the tough practices make the players better prepared for the game. It's always a delicate balance for a coach. You want a fresh team, but you don't want a soft team.

 6. (Less) practice makes (almost) perfect: The Jets eliminated live tackling drills from training camp. So what happened in Week 1? They recorded a league-low one missed tackle, per Next Gen Stats. Go figure.

 Defensive coordinator Brian Duker said they "missed a few" -- it's a subjective stat --- but he still was pleased with the tackling, which was a major issue last season.

 

 7. Learning curve: Top pick David Bailey recorded six quarterback pressures last week, tied for the most by any player in their debut in the Next Gen Stats era, but he was far from perfect. He's still learning how to complement the other rushers, especially in blitz situations, according to coaches.

 Bailey recorded a sack, pushing Titans quarterback Cam Ward out of bounds.

 "Not how I imagined it, but it still counts," said Bailey, who got razzed by some teammates.

 8. Eye on the ball: The defensive backs have been using footballs with painted white tips in their pass-catching drills. It's supposed to help with hand-eye coordination.

 The Jets have gone an NFL record 18 straight games without making an interception, and now their most accomplished interceptor, Minkah Fitzpatrick , has been ruled out  for Sunday because of a groin injury.

 9. Rodgers, revisited: With the Packers in town, this is a good time to look back at the Aaron Rodgers trade in 2023 -- a clear win for Green Bay.

 The Packers received four draft picks in the trade, and they turned them into six picks after additional trades. Five of the six remain on the roster, including defensive starters Lukas Van Ness , Edgerrin Cooper and Evan Williams .

 The Jets got two picks, which became three after a trade. Only one remains -- edge rusher Will McDonald IV . They landed a future Hall of Fame quarterback, but the two-year Rodgers era -- undermined by his torn Achilles in 2023 -- will be remembered as a disappointment.

 10. The last word: "There hasn't been much to root for, and we're all aware of that. We owe it to them." -- Wilson on the fan base
